stories.body:
John Kennedy looks to Trump leaders as he asks how China evidently bypassed export controls for Nvidia’s top AI chips

Invoking Greek mythology, US senator John Kennedy has characterized former Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang ’s reported affair with a suspected Chinese spy as “the most expensive sex since Helen of Troy”.

The Louisiana Republican’s allusion to the legendary figure whose desirability was such that it caused the mythic Trojan war came during an interview on NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday. Host Kristen Welker asked Kennedy, known for his colloquialisms, if US national security was put at risk by Huang’s affair, given the position his company’s chips have occupied at the forefront of the artificial intelligence boom.

Huang stepped down as Nvidia’s CEO on 12 November after allegations surfaced of extramarital relationships with the suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang and two Nvidia employees.

Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, had been executive director of Megaspeed International. Megaspeed facilitated about $12bn in chip sales, in violation of export controls in the US, where the Trump administration has prohibited the selling of advanced AI chips to China.

On Sunday’s edition of CNN’s State of the Union , the Trump administration’s national intelligence director, Jay Clayton, said he suspected China was able to obtain Nvidia’s most advanced AI chips.

He also said on Fox News Sunday: “There are chips that have ended up in places that they should not.”

Kennedy said he was “less interested in … what [Huang] did” than in asking the Trump administration’s commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick , and its treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, about how China was evidently able to circumvent US “export controls”.

“Mr Huang … did what he did. I hope he had a good time. It was the most expensive sex since Helen of Troy,” Kennedy said.

Lutnick has faced scrutiny over allegedly ignoring warnings that Megaspeed was smuggling chips to China. Other administration leaders, including Bessent, wanted to put Megaspeed on a trade blacklist – but the commerce department stalled enforcement of it.

Kennedy said he could only conclude commerce department leaders are either “so incompetent you wouldn’t put them in charge of a food truck” – or “they knowingly allowed this to happen”.

He said he wanted to get Bessent and Lutnick under oath in front of a Senate committee to “answer some hard questions”.

“And if secretary Lutnick is giving our chips away, he needs to stop it, in my opinion,” Kennedy said.

Bessent said on Sunday’s edition of CBS News’s Face the Nation that the Trump administration had been in touch with Nvidia’s temporary management, lead directors and lawyers while trying to find out who was in charge of compliance at the company.

“It behooves Nvidia to move ⁠quickly on this because we want to know what the culture was,” Bessent said on the program.

Kennedy, a former Louisiana state treasurer who began his political career as a Democrat before switching parties and becoming a staunch Trump administration ally, delivers many of the colloquialisms that have become his calling card with a southern US drawl.

Many believe Kennedy resorts to the drawl to come off as folksy – while he holds degrees from Vanderbilt University, the University of Virginia School of Law and the UK’s Oxford University, and is estimated to be one of the wealthiest US senators.

stories.title: GLP-1 drugs could have a surprisingly large environmental payoff
stories.summary: GLP-1 drugs could cut food demand enough to free farmland larger than Italy.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
GLP-1 drugs could cut food demand enough to free farmland larger than Italy.

GLP-1 weight-loss medicines such as Ozempic and Wegovy could affect much more than the waistlines of the people who take them. If widely used, our new research suggests these appetite-suppressing medicines could transform the global food system and free up vast areas of agricultural land.

The global food system is ultimately driven by demand. If people eat less, producers respond, affecting production, prices, trade, and how much land is needed. We used a powerful computer simulation to explore scenarios ranging from GLP-1 use concentrated in high-income countries to widespread global access.

With widespread use of these medicines among adults living with obesity, we estimate that reduced calorie intake could prevent up to 6.6 million deaths each year by 2050, while freeing up as much as 32 million hectares of agricultural land—an area slightly larger than Italy—for other uses.

The biggest effects, however, occurred when reduced calorie intake was combined with a shift toward healthier diets. In this scenario, up to 7 million deaths could be avoided each year by 2050, while around 46 million hectares of agricultural land would have become available for other uses. This suggests that alongside weight-loss medicines, we need to make healthier options more widely available, affordable, and more appealing.

The food system could respond in unexpected ways

Food systems are interconnected across countries. If demand falls in one part of the world, this can affect farming, trade, and food prices elsewhere, with consequences for people who are not taking the medications at all.

Lower demand from GLP-1 users, for instance, could make food cheaper. That sounds positive, but cheaper food could also encourage greater consumption among non-users, offsetting some of the intended benefit. The effects of widespread GLP-1 use, in other words, cannot be understood just by looking at individual patients’ weight loss. They ripple through the global food system.

It’s tempting to read these findings as an argument for putting more people on weight-loss medication. That would miss the bigger picture.

Obesity has often been framed as a “lifestyle disease,” blaming individual people for not having enough willpower . But diets are shaped by what food is available, what it costs, how it’s marketed, where shops are located, and what’s most convenient. In many high-income countries, it is remarkably easy to consume large amounts of cheap, energy-dense food. Society tells people to make healthier choices while surrounding them with an environment that often encourages the opposite.

The UK government-commissioned national food strategy , finalized in 2021, made this point clearly: improving diets can’t simply be about asking individuals to choose better. The wider food environment needs to change to make the better choice the easy one.

Our findings shouldn’t be taken to mean that people living with obesity have a responsibility to lose weight to reduce the environmental impacts of food production. Rather, our research examines the wider consequences that changes in food demand could have across the food system.

Changing the food system alongside medicine

A healthier diet is not necessarily just a diet with fewer calories. It could mean more fruit, vegetables, and other nutritious foods, alongside less excessive consumption of foods linked to poor health. These changes affect not only human health but also agriculture, land use, and the environment.

Rather than asking whether GLP-1 medications or healthier diets are the answer, let’s ask how they can work together. Imagine a food system where healthier foods are affordable and accessible, unhealthy options aren’t relentlessly promoted, agricultural policy supports nutritious and sustainable production, and people who need medical treatment can access it. That combination could be far more powerful than any single intervention.

GLP-1 medicines can play an important role in tackling obesity, but they shouldn’t become a technological fix that allows the wider food system to escape scrutiny. They can help people eat less in an unhealthy food environment, but the long-term goal should be to make it easier and more affordable to have a healthier, more sustainable diet.

The remarkable thing about GLP-1 medications may not be that they change how much food people eat. It may be that they show us, with new clarity, just how closely human health, food production, and environmental health are connected, and how much could be gained if we tackled all three together.

Roslyn Henry is Lecturer, School of Biological Sciences, University of Aberdeen and Peter Alexander is Professor of Global Food Systems, University of Edinburgh .

stories.title: Centrica boss says he is 'hugely concerned' over impact of soaring energy bills
stories.summary: Chris O'Shea says the number of people unable or unwilling to pay their energy bills will increase when prices jump in the new year.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 7 hours ago

The boss of British Gas owner Centrica says he is "hugely concerned" about the impact the expected jump in energy bills in January will have on consumers.

Chris O'Shea told the BBC he thought the number of people unable or unwilling to pay their energy bills would rise when prices go up in the new year.

The new energy price cap to take effect from January will be announced on Wednesday and consultancy Cornwall Insight has forecast it will jump by £443 a year for a typical household.

The government has said some households will get £100 to help with energy bills, but Citizens Advice said it was a "drop in the ocean" while one pressure group called for action on "inflated energy firm profits".

Speaking to the Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme, O'Shea said the predictions for a "substantial increase" in bills from January were "materially correct", adding that the first quarter of the year was the time when most energy was consumed.

"That's right at the point where people will be paying for Christmas and the like. So I am hugely concerned," he said.

O'Shea added there was a "massive problem" with people not paying their bills in the UK, with some not able to pay their bills and an "increasing number of people that are choosing not to pay their bills".

He said the collective impact of that was that "every single electricity consumer, is paying about £1.50, £1.60 a week to cover the cost of people that are not paying their bills, and it's just going to get worse when bills go up".

The amount owed to energy suppliers by households hit £5bn in the April to June period, according to energy regulator Ofgem.

Will I get the £100 energy payment and when will I receive it? Published 28 October

Typical energy bill forecast to go up by £443 a year from January as inflation rate rises again Published 4 days ago

Wholesale energy prices paid by suppliers have been rising this year as a result of the conflict in the Middle East, which has pushed up bills for households.

Cornwall Insight has predicted Ofgem's energy price cap will rise by 26% to £2,166 a year for a typical household from 1 January.

The price cap affects about 20 million households in England, Scotland and Wales and sets a maximum price for each unit of gas and electricity, so the actual level of bills will vary according to energy usage.

The government has said some households will get a £100 payment to help with energy bills, a policy which was announced in the Budget .

The government has also temporarily cut 5% VAT from electricity bills until the end of June next year, which is expected to save the typical household about £45 a year.

But consumer groups have argued the £100 payment announced in the Budget will not be enough for some.

Citizens Advice said it was a "drop in the ocean" and that we would see "cold-related deaths" this winter.

"For someone in a lot of debt, who can't afford their bills, it's not going to touch the sides."

The Fuel Poverty Action Group said the government and Ofgem needed to take stronger action against energy companies.

"Our inflated energy prices are driven by inflated energy firm profits," the group said.

"Government and Ofgem must take stronger action against this blatant profiteering whilst we suffer in cold homes, or are forced into debt."

Energy firms operating in the UK are subject to a windfall tax that was introduced in 2022.

When the windfall tax is added to other taxes levied, it means the overall tax rate on profits earned by oil and gas companies operating in the UK is 78%.

stories.body:
District court in the Hague finds Chinese carmaker infringed on intellectual property of Jaguar Land Rover

Chinese carmaker BYD has been banned from selling its “Defender clone” vehicle in the EU by a court in the Netherlands, after Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) brought a case saying it infringed intellectual property rights.

JLR launched legal action over the seven-seater Ti7 SUV earlier this year after BYD announced on its website that it was taking orders from UK customers for the vehicle. Earlier this month, bailiffs acting for JLR were reported to have seized digital records from BYD’s offices .

“In these summary proceedings, the preliminary relief judge rules that ​the Ti7 infringes the EU design of Jaguar Land Rover ,” said the ruling from the district court in The Hague. “The characteristic ⁠and distinctive elements of the design are reflected in the BYD Ti7.”

The ban will take effect one week after Friday’s ruling, which noted that BYD “currently has no concrete plans to place the Ti7 on the market in the EU”. The judge ruled, however, that the court had no jurisdiction over BYD’s activities in the UK.

BYD’s plug-in hybrid SUV, which has been on sale in China since last September, has been likened by motoring experts to the Land Rover Defender, with the BBC’s Top Gear magazine calling it the “Chinese Defender clone” .

According to BYD’s website : “An unapologetically boxy profile delivers the imposing, chunky design that finds favour among SUV buyers, yet delivers a contemporary look.”

after newsletter promotion

The Ti7 has gone on sale in the UK for £47,995, more than £20,000 cheaper than the Defender, with deliveries to customers due from January 2027.

JLR’s seven-seat Defender is one of the UK’s bestselling cars and is the company’s most popular model. The UK-based carmaker, which is owned by India’s Tata Motors, sold 29,500 Defenders to retail customers between July and September this year, an increase of more than 4,000 on the same period a year earlier.

JLR said in a statement: “We protect our intellectual property and take legal action when necessary. Legal proceedings are ongoing and we won’t be commenting ​further at this time.”

In ​a statement, BYD ⁠said it “strongly disagrees” with the ruling and will appeal. “The BYD Ti7 is the result of BYD’s own independent design work and infringes none of JLR’s rights,” BYD said. “We will pursue every legal avenue to demonstrate that this decision ⁠is incorrect.”

The court also banned BYD from producing the vehicle at its new factory at Szeged in Hungary, which is expected to start producing cars at the end of 2026, until the intellectual property case is resolved.

While many traditional carmakers have complained for some time that Chinese competitors have copied their designs, until now little has been tested in court. It is it relatively rare for European automakers to go to court over infringement of design rights.

However, JLR previously won a legal case to stop Jiangling Motors Corporation selling a copycat vehicle in 2019, after a three-year court battle.

stories.title: Tories would scrap Burnham's deal with EU, deputy leader says
stories.summary: Alex Burghart tells the BBC the agreement will not lead to lower prices in the shops.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Conservative deputy leader Alex Burghart says the deal will not lead to lower prices in shops

Published 8 hours ago

Conservative deputy leader Alex Burghart has said his party would scrap the deal agreed between the UK and the European Union on Friday, if the Tories win the next general election.

The agreement signed by Prime Minister Andy Burnham covers a youth travel scheme, emissions trading and British food exports.

The government has argued scrapping most checks on British food exports will cut costs for businesses and could bring down prices for shoppers.

Burghart told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme the deal was "a dog's dinner", which would not lead to lower prices in the shops and would mean the UK "gives up our ability to set our own rules".

Under the agreement, the UK will also have to follow some EU regulations.

Burghart acknowledged the deal would reduce some trade "friction" but he said it would put a "massive additional burden on the 90% of farmers that don't do any trade with the EU".

Pressed over whether the Conservatives were committed to scrapping the deal if the party wins the next general election, Burghart said: "I don't think that there will be positive outcomes, and yes, we would scrap it."

He added: "I also don't think it is a good idea for a country like Britain to hand over control of its rules to another power and have no say over how those rules are created right into the future."

Food retailers have welcomed the deal, saying it will cut costs, reduce bureaucracy and remove barriers to trade.

However, they have not committed to cutting prices as a direct result of the changes.

The British Retail Consortium has said it does not expect prices on supermarket shelves to fall in response to the deal.

It has said upward pressures on prices remain and will not be alleviated by the agreement.

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband insisted the deal "reduces pressure on trading costs", adding: "They're the things that go into prices."

"It will reduce the costs that the retailers face, all of that Brexit red tape, millions of forms that they were having to fill in, frankly pointlessly, as a result of the bad deal that we had," he told the BBC.

Challenged that the UK was also giving up some powers to set regulations itself, Miliband argued businesses were already "rule takers" from Brussels if they wanted to sell into the European market.

"So they have to abide by the rules of the European Union. But at the same time, because we are not integrated into that market for food and agricultural products, they have to fill in a whole bunch of forms... to confirm that they're observing the right standards, which is frankly crackers," he said.

Under the deal, he said the UK would "be able to shape decisions" for the first time.

Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow Published 2 days ago

'Move on!' Former PMs pile in with advice for Andy Burnham, but will he listen? Published 15 hours ago

Deal with EU not dependent on tuition fees agreement, Miliband says Published 1 day ago

Reform UK has also criticised the UK-EU deal.

Deputy leader Richard Tice told Sky News that while "a few exporting food businesses may benefit", companies that do not export to the EU will still have to align with EU rules.

"Divergence is now our strength. We need to be scrapping net zero so we can bring down energy bills, whereas the EU is still ideologically obsessed with it," he said

"The extra burdens of EU regulations that will be forced through dynamic alignment across all UK businesses is way more than that small net benefit."

Legislation to implement the deal is expected to be introduced in the UK Parliament next week, with the food exports deal in force from 2028.

Elsewhere in the agreement, a new "youth experience scheme" will allow up to 100,000 18 to 31-year-olds to work, study or travel in the EU for up to three years.

The same number of young people from the EU will also be allowed into the UK.

The two sides want to ensure that opportunities under the annual scheme will be available to young people by no later than January 2030.

A proposal from the bloc to lower the level of university tuition fees paid by EU students in the UK has not been agreed and talks on this aspect will continue. Miliband has said Friday's deal is not dependent on an agreement on tuition fees .

The Conservatives have also criticised the youth experience scheme, saying people from the EU will be competing with young Britons struggling to get jobs.

The Liberal Democrats have welcomed the scheme as "a big step forward" but have said "it's nowhere near enough".

The party has called for the UK to rejoin the EU single market and customs union to help cut the cost of living and grow the economy.

stories.title: Trump FCC declares California isn't allowed to enforce phone service rules
stories.summary: FCC preempts state rules that require AT&T to keep offering home phone service.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
FCC preempts state rules that require AT&T to keep offering home phone service.

The Federal Communications Commission ordered California to stop enforcing its Carrier of Last Resort (COLR) rules against AT&T, setting up another battle between the Trump administration and California over the state’s right to enforce its own telecom laws and regulations.

AT&T’s status as a Carrier of Last Resort in California requires it to offer telephone service to any potential customer in its territory. AT&T wants to stop offering basic phone service to new customers and discontinue service for 184,000 residential customers and 15,000 business customers on June 1, 2027.

The order released today granted AT&T’s request to preempt state rules, following up on the FCC’s previous approval of AT&T’s petition to discontinue service. AT&T had tried to achieve the same result in court, but a federal judge rejected its request to override California’s rules in July.

The FCC order probably isn’t the last word, as California could sue the commission. California has stood alone against AT&T, which has received relief from COLR obligations in 20 of the 21 states in its wireline service territory.

Carr: California rules “designed for a bygone era”

“California’s Carrier of Last Resort framework may have made sense when it was established 30 years ago,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement released with today’s order. “But those rules were designed for a bygone era and no longer make sense in today’s competitive, advanced marketplace.”

If AT&T ends service on its old copper lines, many homes and businesses would not be offered modern fiber networks. AT&T claims a wireless home phone service that connects to the cellular network will be good enough, and the FCC agreed.

“The FCC has granted AT&T’s applications to replace legacy voice service with a modern, IP-based alternative in certain areas of the state. California’s state requirements are blocking AT&T from proceeding with a federally authorized transition,” Carr said.

California says its rules allow wireless replacements if they meet the state’s standards for basic phone service, but that AT&T must demonstrate that its wireless phone service would meet the COLR obligations. California’s requirements include flat-rate options for unlimited voice calls, discounted Lifeline rates for eligible low-income customers, and telephone relay service for people who are deaf and hard of hearing.

Gomez: State officials know best

FCC Democrat Anna Gomez voted against the order, saying that state telecom commissions “are often the last line of defense for consumers. They know their communities, they take their complaints, and they answer to the people who rely on these services in a way that a federal agency in Washington cannot always match.”

Gomez said the California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) has an open proceeding on how to modernize its COLR rules, and that the FCC should let that process play out. Large technology transitions work best “when the state regulator is a partner with a real role,” but the FCC is treating the CPUC “as an obstacle to be cleared,” she said.

The CPUC “proceeding is the right place for California to weigh what a modern basic service requirement should look like, with input from the people who will actually be making that switch,” Gomez said. “AT&T has said it does not plan to discontinue service before June 1, 2027, which leaves time for the CPUC to finish its work. Rather than wait, this item tells the CPUC to write its new consumer protections around a federal ruling it opposed.”

In March, the FCC issued an order that made it easier for carriers to discontinue copper networks. The order asserted that state rules are subject to preemption if they conflict with the FCC’s discontinuance authorizations and authority. AT&T cited the order in its lawsuit against California.

Trump officials and telecom companies have been trying to block California’s rules for years. The first Trump administration lost an attempt to preempt state net neutrality laws throughout the country in 2019, and California later defeated ISPs in a lawsuit that challenged its net neutrality law in court.

California’s net neutrality law and other telecom regulations are again being threatened by rules the Trump administration applied to federal grants, but California rejected US demands to stop enforcing its laws this month. In that case, California may have to choose between enforcing its telecom laws and receiving $1.42 billion to deploy broadband to 270,571 locations.

stories.body:
‘Raising growth in every postcode’ has been the PM’s rallying cry but deep regional disparities and rising energy bills pose problems this winter

Andy Burnham faces two, related problems: Britain faces deep regional disparities and it is entering the coldest months of the year with rising inflation.

Since entering Downing Street, raising “growth in every postcode” has been the prime minister’s rallying cry, as he bids to close the gaping chasm in living standards between the richest and poorest areas of the country. But as the war in the Middle East intensifies, the task of spreading prosperity far and wide has only become more difficult.

On Wednesday, the regulator Ofgem is expected to confirm a 26% increase in the energy price cap from January, pushing the annual bill to £2,166 for a typical household.

Rising petrol prices and diesel hitting a record high lifted the UK’s headline inflation rate to 3.6% in October , its highest level in a year. The Bank of England says inflation could hit 5% next year.

It is now half a decade since inflation first went above the 2% target set by the government. Consumer prices have galloped by almost a third over that same time. A return to the target is not expected until 2028 at the earliest.

So far, households have proven surprisingly resilient. Consumer confidence surveys bear this out. Retail sales in October were stronger than expected, even though some of this was driven by a rush to stockpile emergency supplies .

But there is a storm coming. Especially if the El Niño forecast is right and we have a very cold January.

As autumn gives way to winter, low-income households will be hardest hit as the mercury drops. Record numbers of families cannot afford the essentials . The places feeling the pinch most will also be the ones where Burnham has promised to turn things around.

Analysis by the Centre for Cities shows that after the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine, inflation rose most in towns and cities that entered the cost of living crisis in a precarious position. Small towns in the north of England, Midlands and Wales were most exposed. Households in Burnley, Blackburn and Blackpool faced an inflation rate nearly three percentage points higher than those in London, Reading and Cambridge.

Part of this is because the recent inflationary burst has been driven by the price of energy and food, hitting low-income families most because they spend proportionally more on essentials than the wealthiest. And that means some places are harder hit than others because despite the promises of successive governments, Britain’s regional income gaps have barely shifted in three decades .

According to research from the Resolution Foundation, the places that were performing worst in the late 1990s are still at the bottom of the living standards league table a generation later. Disposable incomes in Kensington and Chelsea, at £60,584, remain four-and-a-half times higher than in Leicester, at £13,398.

But in response to the cost of living squeeze, Burnham’s government has, perhaps surprisingly, taken a remarkably blunt approach.

At the autumn budget, the “breathing space” measures announced by John Healey prioritised an across-the-board freeze in fuel duty and £100 energy rebate for every household in council tax bands A to D. The removal of standing charges from gas bills that was also announced will not come into effect until the end of 2027.

after newsletter promotion

The poorest households will benefit from the £150 warm homes discount, on top of a universal VAT cut to electricity bills. But charities warn that overall the government’s limited ambition and relatively poor targeting will fail to meet the moment.

Despite the gloom, there are caveats. After more than three decades of entrenched regional inequality, it would be unreasonable to expect Burnham to turn things around overnight. The legacy of austerity and Britain’s tight fiscal position make his task harder. After years of politicians pursuing a quick fix – often with disastrous consequences – his long-term approach is to be commended.

There are also signs that the outlook could improve. The global oil price has fallen back since the blow to Donald Trump’s authority in the US midterm elections. Brent crude has dropped to about $90 a barrel, down from a peak of close to $120 as recently as the end of October. Growth in Britain’s economy has proven more resilient than feared, helped by the rollout of AI, and unemployment has fallen back in recent months.

Figures show food price inflation was lower than expected in October, at 0.9%, the lowest increase since September 2021. How long this lasts, however, is a moot point, amid expectations of a surge in grocery prices next year linked to higher energy costs and El Niño hitting harvests worldwide.

Andrew Bailey, the Bank’s governor, suggested last week that the pull back in global energy prices could lead headline inflation to fall short of Threadneedle Street’s forecasts for next year.

However, the longer the Iran war rumbles on, the greater the chance of the Bank raising interest rates to keep inflation in check. Financial markets predict three quarter-point increases next year, adding to the financial squeeze for most households. The first could come as early as next month.

In Britain’s poorest postcodes, a tough winter looms. For Burnham’s No 1 political priority, that is a problem.

stories.title: 'Move on!' Former PMs pile in with advice for Andy Burnham, but will he listen?
stories.summary: Theresa May, David Cameron and Tony Blair have weighed in on Burnham's plans on moving closer to the EU, but the prime minister's message itself is not very precise.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
'Move on!' Former PMs pile in with advice for Andy Burnham, but will he listen?

Published 22 November 2026, 06:01 GMT

"Move on!" That's Theresa May's frank instruction to Andy Burnham.

She spent years wrangling with the EU to try to forge a decent Brexit deal before being shoved out of her job by her party. Her leadership was broken by Britain's relationship with Brussels. Now she is warning the current resident of No 10 not to risk the same.

In a rare interview, Baroness May - who presided over negotiations with the EU between 2016 and 2019 - told me Burnham ought to respect the public's decision 10 years ago, not "pat them on their head" as if they gave the wrong answer and should have "another go".

And she said she was "aghast" at what he was doing, dangling the possibility of rejoining the EU, warning it would absorb huge amounts of government effort.

"The hours that have to be put in, it's across the whole of government," she said. "It's not just prime ministerial time, [it's] cabinet ministers' time, officials' time, to-ing and fro-ing on those negotiations."

But while some on his own side are very keen to get on with a campaign to rejoin the EU - and the foreign secretary tells me this option is on the table - May is not the only voice urging caution.

Earlier this month David Cameron also said starting a conversation about rejoining would be "long and painful".

And former Prime Minister Sir Tony Blair has told the Sunday Times this weekend that Britain should only rejoin the European Union if it reforms and allows more innovation on technology .

Theresa May 'aghast' at Burnham's EU plans and says 'Brexit is done' Published 9 hours ago

Burnham promised a "brainstorm" on stage in Brussels yesterday, so what's his plan?

The prime minister's precise message on Europe is, maybe characteristically, not that precise.

From the by-election platform in the summer where he promised not to reopen old arguments and emphasised he was not proposing the UK considers rejoining, to telling the BBC the country could "go all the way" and go back in, to now the promises of a "national conversation" and "brainstorm" with the EU - his words have varied over time.

No 10 plainly wants to move closer to the EU, even if ministers suggest there really is no end fixed position and so this period of working it out is genuine.

They tell me that, in private, "Andy is pretty clearly where he is publicly - he does think it's a big discussion we have to have as a country, it's a national discussion in the context of the 10 year plan, but also has to involve the Europeans".

In other words, even though he makes no secret that he'd like to be in the EU and wishes we had never left, the prime minister won't conclude whether he'll promise to take the country back in until he has a better idea of what relationship he might get out of the EU - and, perhaps too, how the public responds.

Two quick reminders: Burnham has said it wouldn't happen before another election; and, remember there are elections in Europe too. This whole conversation might be transformed if Marine Le Pen becomes the president of France, or the march of other parties who are suspicious of Brussels continues.

Theresa May's fate was decided by Britain's relationship with the EU

The prime minister's body language in Brussels yesterday, though, and his proclamation that it was a "good day" for Britain, displays happiness in government at what they have achieved so far - closer ties on food exports, energy, and allowing young people to live and work more freely on both sides of the Channel.

Despite a last minute classic spanner in the works with a lack of agreement on tuition fees, the UK side feels positive they didn't back down on that issue yesterday, and the broader deals were concluded anyway.

And despite the protestations from the foreign secretary that the deals will all come into force whatever happens on fees, the government will start the legal processes to turn the agreements into law - although there are still plenty of opportunities for other countries to try and unpick them further down the track.

Of course, politicians' reactions to the deal depend which side they were on in the Brexit debate.

The Lib Dems, SNP, Greens and Plaid Cymru plead the case that it's not far enough. The Conservatives complain it's not fair, for example, that British farmers will have to follow EU rules to make life easier for those who trade with the bloc. Reform scream it's a betrayal of the 2016 vote.

But the feeling in government is the summit was a success and showed the EU will allow the UK to pick and choose where to cooperate, and is willing to listen to what the prime minister wants to do next. It's worth saying just as in any negotiation, the EU might always be up for giving if it receives in return.

Burnham announced the deal on Friday with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa

Yet as May warns, doing deals with the European Union is simply, a long hard slog.

And one senior Whitehall source cautions the prime minister not to kid himself that an early feel-good factor doesn't mean future haggling would be a doddle: "British prime ministers can be oddly delusional about the EU - they can get seduced by the hope that good relationships with individual leaders will overcome the ideological inertia in Brussels which is overseen by French and German lawyerly high priests and priestesses.

"European leaders might actually be your friends, but they are not the ones in charge of decision-making in Brussels."

And a former negotiator warns that in his "brainstorm," the prime minister might well find the deal he's concluded this week just about rubs up against the limits of what can be done without going for the full-fat option - telling me: "There isn't much more to go with a strategy of incrementally building on the deal before it becomes quite a binary choice."

They add a reality check for any deal-making with the EU: "The EU have a very set way of doing things, that is more about their own unity than about who they are negotiating with."

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told the BBC the latest deal will come into force regardless of whether the two sides can negotiate a separate tuition fees agreement

Then of course, there is the politics at home. When cornered on this subject the prime minister and his cabinet often say the "British people will be the boss" - going on to cite polling that clearly displays disappointment with Brexit and a discernible interest in going back in.

But that's not the same as polling suggesting the public is demanding the government puts it at the top of the list.

As one senior Labour figure puts it, there has "certainly been a shift - and an openness to have the conversation" about rejoining, but the PM "has to be really careful about locking himself into a manifesto commitment that alienates a lot of people" alongside plenty of voters who might welcome a move.

What of May's warnings about getting tangled up in EU talks at the exclusion of all else?

One government insider from the time asks: "Can you even remember anything else that happened between 2017 and 2020? It's extremely naïve to think he can do all the other things that are extremely pressing, like defence, or Neets, while trying to play out a future with the EU - it won't happen."

It's worth noting, as some ministers do privately, that Burnham himself was not working in Westminster during the most intense struggles over leaving the EU - an advantage perhaps, that he doesn't carry that baggage, or a gap in his experience of how bad it was.

And yet, the prime minister - who, crucially, is confident in his ability to communicate with the public - is plainly resolved on exploring going back into the European Union, and choosing to take that argument on.

After what the government considers to have been a successful summit, that adventure looks more tempting to the many in Labour's tribe who think he is right to do exactly that.

After the last 72 hours, opportunity is knocking - but the warnings from prime ministers past ring out too.

Under May, Brexit affected nearly everyone and everything - trying to go back in under Burnham could perhaps affect everyone and everything too.

stories.summary: In June 2026, the surveillance authority Section 702 of FISA expired absent a consensus among lawmakers over the terms of its reauthorization . Now, with the program set to truly turn off within the next few months, surveillance hawks and national security maximalists are rushing to renew this secretive power by shoving it into a must-pass bill, like a continuing resolution to fund the government or the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) or an end of year, rushed, funding bill to prevent a shutdown. This would be both undemocratic and suppress any real chance at reform. In an effort to prevent that, EFF has singed into a letter with over 25 civil liberties organizations, including the ACLU, Color of Change, and the Brennan Center, to urge Congress not to allow such a significant and dangerous program to be tacked onto a must-pass bill. The letter says: “The NDAA is among the most important bills Congress considers each year. stories.title: Outage Chaos: Who Turned Off All The Computer?
stories.summary: It's been a tough couple of weeks for anyone trying to use email , fly , spend money , use an Apple device *, or do signals intelligence . Technical service outages are nothing new, but why do so many big ones seem to be happening all at once? Are hackers, AI, and international conflicts to blame? And what can we do about it? Since most service interruptions don't make the news, it's hard to get a baseline on how often we see them happen normally. But after a major incident like the Microsoft cloud outage on November 12 , any smaller disruption is more likely to become a story as part of a pattern instead of an isolated incident. We would have heard plenty about the Air Traffic Control problems anyway, but the November 18 disruption to the PlayStation Network might have gotten less attention. There might appear to be a spike or an upward trend in outages, but we can't easily verify that, and the increased coverage will tend to make it seem more significant and interconnected than it necessarily is regardless. One boring reason we might see an uptick in problems right now is the date on the calendar. With Thanksgiving travel, Black Friday, Cyber Monday, Giving Tuesday, and Surveillance Sunday (we assume) all coming up, organizations often schedule major system updates for the first three weeks of November. This helps them prepare for holiday traffic, and lets them shift the outage risk to the time before those dates when they may consider it far more important to maintain reliable service. While none of these particular outages have yet been directly attributed to AI ( or to malicious hackers ), bank CEOs and the NSA briefed congress and reportedly attributed at least some of them to rushed attempts to patch vulnerabilities found by AI. That’s understandable: all software updates carry risk, and companies and governments are having to deploy more updates, and faster, than they’ve ever needed to before. Some of those updates are to important infrastructure, where an outage would be very disruptive, but the impact of leaving vulnerabilities unpatched would be even worse. stories.body:
All options open in future talks, says Ed Miliband, while prime minister hails ‘a good day for Britain and Europe’

The UK rejoining the EU could be on the table in informal discussions between Andy Burnham and European leaders in Brussels, Ed Miliband has said.

The foreign secretary said “all options” would be examined in the process, after the prime minister agreed deals on trade and young people with the bloc on Friday.

Agreements on food and drink standards, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme were announced after talks this week. Under the plans, 100,000 young Britons will be allowed to live, work, study and travel in the EU, with similar access for Europeans in the UK.

Burnham said the agreement would add 0.5% to the UK’s GDP, a £17bn boost to the British economy.

Miliband said Burnham would have further “brainstorming” discussions with the EU in the next year about what could happen next. He said the agreements this week were the limit of what could be done before the next general election.

However, the trio of deals could be derailed in six months, as the EU threatened to block them unless the UK allows European students to pay domestic-level fees to study at British universities.

Miliband said in an interview for the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that “all the options will be on the table” when pressed on whether rejoining the bloc would be considered, adding: “We will look at the benefits and the costs of all the different options.”

Since entering government in 2024, Labour has stuck to the “red lines” in its manifesto, which stated the party would not rejoin the single market or customs union. It also ruled out freedom of movement.

Burnham has previously said he wants to see the UK rejoin the EU in his lifetime.

The prime minister will use the announcement of his 10-year plan before Christmas to explore how the UK could get closer to the EU after the next election. Informal discussions will take place with Brussels before next year’s UK-EU summit.

Miliband said he accepts the result of the 2016 vote but “the world has changed massively”.

“Europe is changing too, so we’ve got to look at what that means,” he said. “It’s not about this parliament, we’re respecting the red lines in this parliament.”

He also denied the deal with the EU would rely on progress in discussions on students from the bloc coming to the UK. It has been reported that a proposal from the bloc to lower the level of tuition fees paid by EU students in the UK has not been agreed.

Miliband told the BBC it was “absolutely clear” the agreements on food exports, energy and youth mobility would apply, even though there has not been a deal on tuition fees.

The foreign secretary said: “The dates are set out in 2028 when these things are coming in, we’re introducing legislation in parliament, so definitely.”

On Friday, Burnham said the agreement represented a “good day for Britain and Europe”. He said the agreements answer “the biggest challenges of our times and the biggest worries that people have”, citing the cost of living, lack of economic growth, illegal immigration and challenges facing young people.

“The deal is done. It is there in black and white in front of you,” Burnham said, adding that the legislation would enter parliament next week.

The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, played down the disagreement, saying she was “confident we are going to find a solution”. About the further discussions, she said: “We welcome this brainstorming, so count on us.”

The environment secretary, Angela Eagle, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme on Saturday the deal was good for farmers. “(It) will open up new markets. They’ll be able to import and export. This is a win-win for the UK. We will dissolve a lot of the friction and costs at the border for UK agriculture and food.”

stories.summary: The US president provided little detail on the potential policy, saying others in his team were hearing about it for the first time.

Trump says he won't allow American companies to build data centres "outside" the US

Published 20 November 2026

Donald Trump has said he will ban US companies from building AI data centres overseas, threatening a "tremendous tax" for tech firms who do so.

"We're going to keep it all in this country," the US president said, while providing little detail on the potential policy he said others in his cabinet were hearing about for the first time.

Data centres were a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction.

Tech giants including Meta and Google have entered agreements to build data centres overseas. It remains unclear how such a policy would be enforced if it was brought in.

"We're not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country," Trump told reporters in a press briefing following his return from his trip to Asia.

"Because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen."

But whether that idea will become policy remains unclear.

"I don't know if that's a breaking story, but I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now, they're here," he said.

Trump floated the policy after saying the US was leading on data centre construction, and he would not allow China to beat the US when it came to AI - which he calls super intelligence, or SI.

It also follows an announcement earlier this week that would restrict the export of advanced computer chips and who can access the computing power provided by them.

Washington on Monday announced firms would require a licence to buy advanced chips, so US officials can monitor whether they are being used to serve Chinese companies or they are being smuggled into China.

The move will impact South East Asian countries that have invested heavily in data centres, as Chinese companies seek to rent computing power from overseas.

Why Canada is embracing AI data centres while the US pushes back Published 2 days ago

Data centres are crucial to the AI boom. The vast warehouse-style buildings house the advanced computer chips and servers that are needed to run AI programmes such as Claude and ChatGPT.

As of April there were about 3,000 data centres across the US, with another 1,500 in various stages of approval and construction, according to the Pew Research Centre.

Many of them are built in rural areas, and concerns about issues including noise pollution and energy consumption helped drive Democratic candidates promising tougher rules on data centre construction to wins on 3 November.

"You ought to take advantage of the data centres. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but take advantage don't shut them off," Trump said.

"We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places. They have energy and they have everything. They're tremendous assets."

Large tech firms - often called AI hyperscalers due to the size of their investments in AI - have also been branching out, and Canada has made moves to step in to offer itself as an alternative location for these sites, with less local pushback against projects so far.

Meta has already broken ground on a data centre , external in the province of Alberta, and Anthropic has signed a long-term agreement to lease a proposed data centre in Nova Scotia.

The BBC has reached out to Meta for comment on Trump's remarks.

In September Google announced a €13bn ($15bn: £11bn) investment in AI infrastructure in Finland, which included funding for three data centres.

Last month, building work for two of those centres was halted due to concerns over the clearance of more than 300 hectares of forest.

Trump called out the build in Finland specifically, saying his administration was "not allowing that to happen".

Google has been contacted for comment.

stories.body:
For many women, childbirth is the one of the most meaningful and joyous moments of life. For some, though, the experience can be overshadowed by fear, neglect or a loss of dignity in a health facility. A woman arrives at a hospital in labour, anxious, in pain, and relies entirely on the care received.

Most women in Rwanda ( 98% in 2025) give birth in health facilities. Little attention has been paid, however, to the quality of care these mothers get.

I’m a nurse-midwife educator and researcher . In a recent paper , my colleagues and I studied the extent of disrespect and abuse experienced by women during childbirth in Rwanda. The problem has been reported in several countries worldwide, including Rwanda . Studying the local context provides a better understanding of how it manifests.

We surveyed 246 mothers shortly after they had given birth at a public hospital in the capital, Kigali. We asked them to respond to a series of questions on how they were treated.

Seven in 10 mothers in our study reported experiencing at least one form of disrespect during labour or childbirth. Our definitions of disrepect included:

insults or physical violence

being left alone when they needed help

being treated without dignity

not being told what was happening to them.

Our findings represent the experiences of women in just one Rwandan hospital. Nevertheless, they highlight an important concern about women’s experiences during childbirth. Caring for a mother’s life and delivering a healthy baby are essential, but the way a woman is treated while receiving that care matters too.

Some women may become reluctant to seek care in the future because of a previous negative experience. This can negatively affect the health of a mother and her baby.

Our research is already influencing healthcare policy in Rwanda. In 2026, I supported the Rwanda Biomedical Centre as a consultant in revising the national obstetric and neonatal care guidelines . While the final version is yet to be published, the revisions formally integrate respectful maternity care, define its principles, provide practical guidance, and identify unacceptable forms of disrespect and abuse during childbirth.

This moves respectful care from an aspiration to an accountable national health standard.

To achieve this, Rwanda needs to ensure continuous training, provide enough staff and resources, and make sure every woman is treated with kindness and respect during childbirth. Hospitals should listen to women’s experiences and use their feedback to improve services.

Good maternity care is not only about helping mothers deliver babies. It is also about treating every woman with dignity and respect, and allowing her to make decisions about her care.

What women experienced

We asked the women in our study if they had experienced physical abuse, such as being slapped or hit, or verbal abuse, such as being insulted, shouted at, humiliated or spoken to rudely during labour.

We also asked if they were left unattended, received information on what was being done to them and gave consent before care was provided. We asked if their privacy and confidentiality were respected, and if they were detained in the hospital because they couldn’t pay their bill.

Read more: What drives abuse of women in childbirth? We asked those providing the care

The most frequently reported experiences included abandonment (77 respondents) and receiving undignified care (76 respondents). This means the woman wasn’t treated with kindness, respect and humanity during childbirth. We also found that 65 respondents were not provided with information on the care received.

A smaller number reported more serious experiences. These include being beaten, pinched or kicked. There were also reports of having an episiotomy (a surgical cut made in the area between the vaginal opening and the anus during vaginal childbirth) repaired without anaesthesia, or undergoing procedures without their consent.

Why respectful care matters

The World Health Organization recognises eliminating disrespect and abuse during childbirth as a global health priority. This is because it protects women’s rights, improves the safety and quality of care for mothers and babies, encourages women to use health facilities, and builds trust between women and healthcare workers.

This is backed up by research from around the world that shows that disrespectful treatment during childbirth can contribute to fear and shame , loss of trust and emotional distress .

Read more: Obstetric violence: abuse during childbirth is widespread, but the first step to fighting it is naming it

Childbirth experiences are also remembered and shared. A woman may tell her sister, friend, daughter or neighbour what happened to her. A negative experience can, therefore, influence how other women view health facilities and their confidence in seeking professional care. This could lead to an increase in the deaths of mothers and newborns.

What’s gone wrong?

It would be easy to look at our findings and blame individual healthcare workers. However, the problem is more complex.

Disrespectful maternity care isn’t only caused by how healthcare workers treat mothers. It can also result from problems within the healthcare system .

Poor hygiene, inadequate infection prevention, shortages of essential supplies, and overcrowded facilities can make it difficult to provide safe and respectful care. For example, women may lose their privacy when hospitals lack curtains or partitions.

Mothers who experience the loss of a baby or other serious complications may also suffer emotionally when there are no trained professionals available to provide psychological support.

Therefore, preventing disrespect and abuse during childbirth requires strengthening the entire health system through better facilities, adequate resources, sufficient staffing and improved quality of maternity services.

What can be done?

Based on our findings , we make a number of recommendations.

Firstly, hospitals should strengthen systems for receiving and responding to complaints. This could include conducting surveys to measure the satisfaction of mothers or using suggestion boxes to receive feedback on the quality of care received. Health facility managers should also regularly assess women’s experiences of care.

Read more: Africa can and must do more to support nurses and midwives

Secondly, healthcare workers need practical support and training that goes beyond simply telling them to “be respectful”. Training should involve teaching providers to communicate clearly, involve women in care decisions, protect privacy, and understand how their words and actions affect women during vulnerable moments.

Thirdly, lasting improvements require broader action. These include better working conditions for healthcare workers, stronger leadership and accountability, community involvement, and efforts to remove barriers within health facilities.

stories.body:
South Africa’s child support grant provides financial support to more than 13 million children in low-income households . It has become an essential part of the country’s social safety net, helping families meet basic needs and invest in their children’s health and education.

The grant ends in the month of their 18th birthday , when they are no longer legally children.

However, for many young South Africans, turning 18 brings little immediate financial independence, especially when faced with a labour market with exceptionally high youth unemployment . More than half of young people 15-24 who are actively looking for work cannot find a job . When the grant support is withdrawn, young people may have no reliable way to replace it with earnings. They may still be at school, trying to secure a place at university or college, or preparing to enter a labour market in which opportunities are scarce.

Losing R580 (US$35) a month can be a financial shock for households already struggling to make ends meet.

Considerable research has examined the benefits of receiving cash transfers . A recent review of the literature found strong positive average effects on a range of indicators, including school enrolment, food security, mental health, and child height-for-age. But surprisingly little attention has been paid to what happens when this support is withdrawn.

Our team of development economists from Stellenbosch University set out to address this in a recently published paper , examining what happens to mental health when young people lose access to child support grants. Theory suggests that it should have an impact on mental health, especially if it occurs during an important and often stressful life transition.

We found that teenagers experienced a substantial deterioration in mental health when they aged out of the grant. Based on these findings, we argue that the design of social support must consider exits more carefully. If support ends abruptly and traumatically, some of its gains may be at risk.

The impact

Our study followed almost 8,000 adolescents and young adults using data from South Africa’s National Income Dynamics Study , covering 2010 to 2017. By comparing young people before and after the eligibility cutoff and examining changes over time, we could distinguish the effects of losing the grant from the broader challenges of growing older.

We compared young adults a few months (less than a year) before their 18th birthday to young adults a few months (less than a year) after their 18th birthday. This window is selected to minimise the statistical error in the model.

Depressive symptoms were measured using the Center for Epidemiologic Studies 10-item self-report Depression Scale . It is a measure designed to assess symptoms of depression, with scores indicating the severity of depressive symptoms. It includes being bothered by things that don’t usually bother you, trouble keeping your mind on things you were doing, feeling depressed, not feeling hopeful about the future, feeling fearful, and struggling to “get going”.

We found a substantial increase in depressive symptoms when young people aged out of the grant. The deterioration was particularly pronounced immediately around the age threshold.

One reason for the increase in depressive symptoms was that just after losing the grant, young people were more likely to be looking for work compared with young people who were only a few months younger and who were still receiving the grant. This points towards the fact that these young people were experiencing pressure to find work, possibly to compensate for the loss of the grant.

The effects appeared particularly pronounced among young people in poorer urban households and those with limited alternative income sources. As expected, losing support is especially difficult when households have few financial resources to fall back on.

One interesting finding was that young people were more likely to look for work after losing the grant. At first glance, this might seem positive. After all, finding employment is an important step towards financial independence. But the interpretation is less straightforward in a country where jobs are exceptionally difficult to find. Among young people aged 15-34 about one in 10 are classified as discouraged workers, meaning that they are no longer actively looking for work, despite not having a job, and not being enrolled for further training or a qualification.

Increased job searching may reflect financial pressure rather than improved opportunities. Young people may feel compelled to look for work before completing their education or acquiring the skills they need.

Our study cannot establish that increased job searching explains the deterioration in mental health, but the findings are consistent with the possibility that young people respond to the loss of financial support by trying to replace it, often in difficult circumstances.

Is support being withdrawn too early?

The child support grant is designed to protect children from poverty and improve their prospects during their formative years. Yet the grant is withdrawn at an age when many are still economically dependent and face substantial barriers to completing their education and entering employment.

Adolescence and early adulthood are particularly important periods for mental health, education and the development of skills. Difficulties experienced during this transition can have lasting consequences . Poor mental health can make it harder to study, search for work and sustain employment. This raises the possibility that withdrawing support too abruptly may undermine some of the investments made in children during their earlier years.

We are mindful that South Africa faces severe fiscal constraints, and any extension of the child support grant would need to be carefully costed and evaluated. One option would be to consider transitional support for particularly vulnerable young people who are still completing school or moving into further education, training or employment. Another would be to strengthen the links between social grants and programmes that help young people make these transitions.

There may also be scope for phasing out financial assistance more gradually, rather than withdrawing it abruptly at a fixed age.

stories.body:
Carbon Captured

The proposed solution to climate change is based on scientific models that offer little transparency into how they’re made. So I spoke with three leading climate modelers about their work — and what assumptions go into it.

You see the promise on airline booking screens, shipping boxes, electronics and grocery aisles: “Carbon neutral.” “Net zero.” “Climate pledge friendly.” Those labels rest on the comforting premise that even when companies and countries keep burning fossil fuels, the resulting pollution can be canceled out by simply capturing the carbon and locking it away.

Recently, along with my colleagues at ProPublica and Drilled, I investigated how the world came to rely so heavily on this premise , particularly in the technology known as carbon capture and storage . CCS aims to trap carbon dioxide that would otherwise be warming the atmosphere and pump it thousands of feet below Earth’s surface, where, ideally, it stays put. The oil industry has long favored the idea.

At the industry’s prodding, the United Nations has effectively endorsed the idea that the technology can work at a massive scale.

Over the last two weeks, world leaders and negotiators met in Antalya, Turkey, for the U.N.’s annual flagship climate summit, where nations hash out global commitments to curb warming. A central foundation of these negotiations — and many of those carbon-neutrality labels and climate pledges — is the expectation that we can bury billions of tons of CO2 a year, an operation that would rival today’s entire global oil industry within just a couple of decades.

Yet our reporting found that expectation rests on thin evidence. After three decades of development, only 12 large-scale geologic storage projects have ever been built, and at least seven have underperformed or failed. Last year, the world buried less CO2 underground than a single large power plant emits annually.

Why do world leaders keep staking climate policy on a technology that remains unproven?

Because the models they all rely on to guide their approach have already presumed that it will work.

I spoke to more than 100 experts for this series, including several members of the wildly powerful group of people who build and run those models. Their simulations of the economy and environment map out how specific choices, like retiring coal plants or electrifying vehicles, could prevent warming catastrophic enough to submerge cities like Miami. Which means that if they’re wrong, Miami could pay the price.

One chart laid bare to me exactly how wrong they’ve been about CCS. It compares one prominent model’s projections for CCS with their projections for solar power, a technology so abundantly tested and proven that you can likely spot a panel out the nearest window:

Carbon Capture Capacity Has Never Come Close to Projections

Meanwhile, solar electricity production has grown rapidly, far outpacing projections.

I wanted to understand what could possibly account for such a disparity. But the problem is the models are opaque: Unlike most scientists, who trade in public, peer-reviewed studies, modelers aren’t required to document every assumption they build into their influential simulations.

So I tracked down the leaders of the world’s three most influential climate models — one based in the Netherlands, another in Germany and a third in Austria — and asked. Here’s what I learned:

Climate models assume it’s easy and efficient to capture carbon. It’s not.

Public data is hard to come by, but several analyses have found the real capture rates are far lower than the industry has promised. Yet the models calculate as much as a 92% success rate. When I pointed out this discrepancy to Keywan Riahi, who leads the Austrian model, he insisted that capturing concentrated CO2 from industrial emissions “is not high-tech, this is very easy to do.” Riahi told me the models assume a high rate of capture because they factor in incentives such as payouts from carbon taxes and large government subsidies. Add those incentives, he argues, and the capture rates would increase.

They don’t account for problems that come up in real-world practice.

In project after project, operators have struggled to inject as much carbon into the earth as they say they can. For instance, at Chevron’s Gorgon natural gas processing plant in Australia, billed as the largest CCS operation on Earth, clogged wells and pressure spikes have forced operators to release most of their CO2 straight into the air. As it stands, only the German model, led by Jessica Strefler, assumed there’d be any limit to how much CO2 operators could inject underground at once. But, she told me, there is no good data to work from, and she pegged the limit based on “expert interviews” with people in the industry.

They assume the Earth is a bottomless geologic landfill.

Modelers took that cue from a rosy 2005 U.N. report, which I’d learned had been written at the behest of Saudi Arabia and allied petrostates, that portrayed underground storage space as practically limitless. (The U.N.’s climate science body has said it stands by the report. Scientists who contributed to the report also defended their work. Authors and editors from Saudi Aramco, Chevron and Shell joined scientists in writing it; the companies did not respond to requests for comment.) Yet just last year, a paper in the journal Nature warned that the earth’s capacity to absorb CCS could be far more limited once you rule out pumping the gas beneath cities, into earthquake zones and under the deepest parts of the oceans. If CCS ever worked at the scale modelers imagine, the paper found, the Earth could run out of room as soon as early next century. Riahi, himself a co-author on that paper, conceded that although his model presumes the earth’s capacity for carbon storage is literally infinite, the real potential may be “smaller.”

They assume that stored CO2 will stay put.

Scientists warn that even tiny annual leak rates over longtime horizons could undermine a storage site’s climate benefit. Our investigation found two large-scale sites that have leaked, one all the way to the surface. Surely the models all factor in this risk? I asked Detlef van Vuuren, leader of the Dutch model, if his did so. His one-word answer: “Nope.”

The models all assume CCS gets more affordable over time, though real-world costs have steadily climbed.

When I asked Strefler if it makes sense to assume our children and grandchildren will pay big bucks to suck CO2 out of the air, even though today governments won’t spend pennies to avoid emitting that pollution, she said: “If a country is not willing to do that, I don’t see how they would be willing to” pay for CO2 removal.

In short, the modelers overlooked decades of underperformance, inflated capture rates, evidence of leaks and finite underground storage, all while assuming future generations will willingly bankroll an increasingly expensive industry. They pointed to a mix of legitimate studies to support those assertions. They also pointed to unreviewed white papers, casual chats with industry insiders and the 2005 U.N. report — of which van Vuuren was an author. Van Vuuren said his team is working to revise some of its assumptions, but he generally sees no technical reason why CCS cannot work, or should be excluded from the possibilities his model considers. He said it is a policy decision whether countries wish to invest the dollars and effort to make it happen.

One way to look at the model projections is as recipes for the future. Seen this way, the modelers’ argument is that their job is to assemble a cookbook, not tell us how each recipe tastes. In other words, the models merely show that if CCS works and is used at an extraordinary scale, it is possible to hit climate targets. And the modelers told ProPublica and Drilled that the delay in climate action has left few other tools to do so — and so they include CCS.

A good recipe, though, cannot rely on imaginary ingredients. If we’re making unrealistic assumptions, why not include the possibility that aliens will appear and hand us a solution to climate change, I asked Riahi, half joking.

“You can quote me that I think carbon dioxide removal is more likely than an alien,” Riahi said.
