stories.title: A Texas Police Department Got $100K After a Single Immigration Arrest. It Stands to Earn Much More.
stories.summary: The post A Texas Police Department Got $100K After a Single Immigration Arrest. It Stands to Earn Much More. appeared first on ProPublica .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.imageAlt: A tan concrete building with tall windows, metal awnings over glass double doors bearing sheriff seals, and green shrubbery along a brick-paved street in bright daylight.
stories.body:
The 287(g) immigration enforcement program funnels millions in federal dollars to local law enforcement with few strings attached. In Texas, cash-strapped police departments are spending the money on things like new equipment and vehicles.

Co-published with KXAN and The Texas Tribune

Last spring, the police chief in a tiny North Texas suburb called Pantego went before his town council with what might have sounded like an audacious pitch to bring in more money for policing.

His department could accept the federal government’s offer to get into the business of immigration enforcement.

“I won’t say there’s unlimited funding, but there’s quite a bit of money in the fund,” Pantego Police Chief Robert Rife said during the April meeting in which council members approved an agreement with Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

He was right. After a single immigration arrest this past June, Pantego received $100,000.

It stands to earn much more.

Rife predicted in his presentation to the council that federal grants could bring in an additional $720,000 for the 2,500-resident town a few miles east of Fort Worth. For perspective, combined with the money it had already received, that’s roughly equivalent to 40% of the town’s $2.1 million police budget last year.

Pantego is one of 429 law enforcement agencies in the state as of mid-September that have entered into agreements with ICE as part of President Donald Trump’s efforts to accelerate deportations. Texas leads the nation in these partnerships, known as 287(g) agreements, which authorize local officers to make immigration arrests during their normal course of duty. A key incentive for local governments across the country has long been the funding that comes with participation .

The federal program funnels millions of dollars to local law enforcement while requiring few measurable results and little tracking of how the money is spent. KXAN reviewed minutes from nine local government meetings and found that, over and over again, Texas law enforcement officials sold the program to their local elected leaders as a boon for their cash-strapped departments.

The same month Pantego decided to join the program, for example, the police chief in the small suburb of Hollywood Park near San Antonio made a similar pitch to his city council. The city “actively profits on payroll for the time spent,” he said.

And in Smith County in East Texas, Sheriff Larry Smith told county commissioners that “equipment, use of fuel, mileage and things of that nature” could all be reimbursed, plus there would be $100,000 for two new vehicles and money for overtime.

“How often do the feds offer us money for anything?” Smith County Commissioner John Moore asked.

“Not very often,” the sheriff responded. He declined to speak with KXAN.

Austin-based immigration attorney Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch worries that local law enforcement will become dependent on the financial incentives, making it difficult to pull away from the program in the future.

“I’m concerned about what this money is going to be doing to the mindset of these small police departments,” she said.

In the Texas Panhandle, Hartley County Sheriff Chanze Fowler said nearly all the federal funding his department receives supports its regular operations, in addition to immigration work.

The sheriff’s office recorded 54 arrests under 287(g) authority from January to early July, most for minor traffic and vehicle violations, according to records obtained by KXAN. It received more than $205,000 during that time. By this past summer, it had spent about $30,000 on things like wages, extra pay for officers who became 287(g) certified, payroll taxes, retirement funds and “fleet purchases.”

Almost all of the 287(g)-related funds “go towards items needed for our everyday job,” Fowler said.

Other local city and law enforcement officials said the additional funds help officers protect their communities and carry out core duties. ICE did not respond to a request for an interview for this story but instead provided a statement that explained the program. Its website says the program targets dangerous criminal offenders.

Pantego officials have declined to answer KXAN’s questions about the department’s involvement with the program since August, despite repeated attempts to reach the mayor, town council, city manager and police chief by phone, email and in person.

“We are not interested in interviewing at this time,” said City Manager Leslie Galloway, the only official to respond.

Ammon Blair, a senior fellow for the Texas Public Policy Foundation, a conservative think tank that supports the program, acknowledged the money can help departments operating on thin budgets, including helping to pay for overtime. But he said there should be more oversight of how the federal money is spent.

KXAN obtained service agreements between ICE and the Smith County Sheriff’s Office and the police department in Bullard, Texas, a town of about 5,300 people in East Texas. The agreements allow either party to terminate with 60 days’ notice. None indicate that the federal government can reclaim funding if an agreement is terminated.

That was one of the selling points in Pantego. The department could get federal funding and eventually drop out of the program without penalty and keep the equipment already purchased, the police chief told town council members. All it had to do was make at least one immigration arrest.

Between the end of April and mid-June, it made two.

“Are You a U.S. Citizen?”

Local law enforcement agencies that join forces with ICE can choose among three models, two of which focus on identifying people already in jail who may be subject to deportation.

Trump revived the third kind, called the task force model, at the beginning of his second term. Task force agreements often worry civil and immigrants’ rights groups because of the model’s problematic track record: ICE started phasing them out in 2012, after Department of Justice investigations revealed that sheriff’s offices participating in the model had committed civil rights violations.

But task force agreements can also be lucrative.

Agencies can receive federal reimbursement for salaries, overtime and benefits for “conducting purposeful and intentional” immigration enforcement activities once the contract starts, according to a service agreement obtained by KXAN.

They can also get recurring quarterly incentive payments and one-time stipends for equipment, technology and vehicles, though federal memoranda and agreements obtained by KXAN don’t specify what agencies can purchase.

The Department of Homeland Security stopped renewing task force model agreements during the Obama administration after federal investigations revealed civil rights violations involving sheriffs’ offices in Arizona and North Carolina .

Since Trump’s return to office, the model has become the most common of the three agreement types. At least 241 task force model agreements were signed in Texas in 2026 alone, compared to just 30 combined for the other models in that time period, according to ICE participation data from September.

Smith County was among the first in Texas to sign on after the president reinstated the task force model in early 2025.

Moore, the only member of Smith County ’s Commissioners Court who agreed to speak with KXAN, explained why he thought the commissioners wanted to partner.

His first word: “budgetary.”

“Any kind of training that any of our departments need to have, or are required to have, costs money, and it’s rare that we get an opportunity to get funding for training from outside county taxes,” Moore said. “Any time we can save the taxpayers money, I’m all for it.”

Smith County got more money than any other of the 93 Texas law enforcement agencies whose funding KXAN reviewed. The sheriff’s office received nearly $2.2 million in federal 287(g) funding from January 2025 to June 2026, according to records obtained by KXAN. That’s equivalent to about 12% of its budget for fiscal year 2025.

Smith, the sheriff, told the Commissioners Court last November that although vehicles purchased with that money would be used for the 287(g) program, “that doesn’t mean, if we’re out here, we won’t run to another call or take another call that comes across the radio. We will do that. We try not to separate 287(g) from our other law enforcement duties. We do it all together.”

About 120 of 198 licensed officers in the Smith County Sheriff’s Office participated in the program. Together, they conducted 124 immigration enforcement actions between October 2025 and July. KXAN requested a list of 287(g) stops from the department, in addition to any associated charge. Smith County listed no associated criminal charge for more than 100 of these stops.

Jose Rodriguez and his 23-year-old son, Pablo Rodriguez, were among those affected.

One afternoon in late June, the pair cruised along Loop 323, a circular segment of highway in Tyler, a city of 113,000 people in East Texas. They’d spent hours working in the summer heat at a construction job and were headed to Chick-fil-A to pick up lunch for their family.

Then red and blue lights appeared behind them. The law enforcement agent said that he’d pulled their black extended-cab work truck over because of a missing license plate on the trailer attached to the pickup and a missing dual-wheel mud flap.

Body and vehicle camera footage showed the detective requesting that Jose Rodriguez get out of the truck. “Any English at all?” the detective later asked. Jose Rodriguez raised his right hand, holding his thumb and index finger close together.

“Un poquito?” the detective asked, followed by, “Are you a U.S. citizen?”

The man shook his head and answered. “No.”

Seconds later, the detective pulled Jose Rodriguez’s hands behind his back and put him in handcuffs.

He was eventually taken from the Smith County jail to an ICE detention facility, about two hours west of Tyler. His son, who is a U.S. citizen, said Jose Rodriguez was detained for about three months before being deported to Mexico.

KXAN could find no criminal convictions or arrests on his record when the Smith County detective took him into custody in June.

“Just like that, he’s gone,” Pablo Rodriguez later told KXAN. “My dad’s gone.”

Law enforcement officers, Pablo Rodriguez said, “portray us as criminals, rapists, violent people. We’re not that. We’re just regular people trying to find a better life. The only difference is our skin. That’s pretty much it.”

The Future of the Program in Texas

Elections earlier this month have left the 287(g) program’s future uncertain, at least in Texas.

While the Trump administration has reached agreements with local law enforcement to work with immigration officials, Congress has broader oversight authority. That includes decisions about funding. In January, Democrats will take over both chambers of Congress and many, including freshman Texas Sen. James Talarico, have criticized ICE tactics. It’s unclear, however, how much of their focus will be on immigration enforcement and specifically on the 287(g) program.

More locally, state Sen. Charles Schwertner, the Republican lawmaker who authored a measure in 2025 that required most Texas sheriff’s offices to participate in the program, wants to expand the mandate during the coming legislative session to include other law enforcement agencies, like police departments. So does the conservative think tank where Blair works.

But support for such legislation may be harder to get after November’s midterm election.

Schwertner retained his state Senate seat, and Republicans maintained their majority in that chamber, but Democrats took control of the governor’s mansion and the state House of Representatives for the first time in a generation. Any new bills would require legislative approval from both chambers and the governor’s signature, or enough legislative support to override a veto.

In a press release well before the election, Democrat Gina Hinojosa called on Gov. Greg Abbott to “demand accountability from the Trump administration and stop enabling ICE operations that are terrorizing communities and violating the law.” The release did not mention the 287(g) program by name. Hinojosa beat Abbott in this month’s election and will take over as governor in January. She did not respond to a request for comment for this story.

The state program could also be affected by this month’s election of Democrats Nathan Johnson , who won the race for state attorney general, and Sarah Eckhardt , who won her bid to become state comptroller.

Johnson, as a state senator, opposed the mandate that sheriffs’ offices participate in the program. He will inherit responsibility for enforcing the law, which requires most sheriffs to seek agreements with ICE by Dec. 1. Johnson said he will use his discretion in deciding whether to sue sheriffs who fail to comply if they have “legitimate law enforcement reasons for not having a 287(g) agreement.”

He also questioned the state attorney general’s continued participation in the program. Current Attorney General Ken Paxton signed a 287(g) task force model agreement in February 2025.

“The attorney general’s office has tremendous, vast responsibilities,” Johnson said. “Never included among them since the creation of this state was outsourcing your employees to a federal agency for a purpose in which we’re not trained or qualified and which distracts me from the mission of my office.”

Johnson didn’t entirely rule out working with ICE in some capacity if it allowed his office to investigate crimes committed by ICE agents in Texas.

Eckhardt, meanwhile, will take over oversight of a $20 million grant program that state lawmakers created two years ago to help sheriff’s offices cover any costs of participation in the 287(g) program not reimbursed by the federal government. By late September, the comptroller’s office had awarded more than $6.5 million to 78 sheriff’s offices, according to figures obtained by KXAN.

During her campaign, Eckhardt warned that expenses for the program could eventually fall on local taxpayers, calling it “unsustainable.” After winning her seat, she said she would “do a 287(g) audit to show how that expense is driving up property taxes.”

Even if state leaders don’t expand the participation requirement or remove the current mandate, departments can choose to keep collecting federal money to enforce immigration law.

In Fayette County southeast of Austin, Sheriff’s Lt. David Beyer told KXAN that the 287(g) funding his office had already received totaled about $800,000, which helps purchase equipment it can also use for ordinary police work.

“If they want to pay us extra to do that job,” Beyer said, “we’re more than happily going to accept those funds, because that saves our taxpayers money.”

American actor James Stewart stands behind Donna Reed, gesturing with a handful of money while speaking to a group of townspeople in a still from the film, 'It's A Wonderful Life,' directed by Frank Capra, 1946. (RKO Pictures/Courtesy of Getty Images)

Frank Capra’s It’s a Wonderful Life is remembered for its faith in institutions, community, and public trust. Paraguay’s recent banking crisis offers a darker sequel. The collapse of Ueno Bank exposed not simply the failure of a financial institution but the consequences of a political system in which power, influence, and economic interests had become increasingly intertwined.

But the banking crisis did not create Paraguay’s underlying problem. It exposed something that had been developing for years: the growing capture of political and economic institutions by a powerful political machine centered on former president Horacio Cartes and his political protégé, Santiago Peña who became Paraguay’s president in 2023.

Paraguay’s banking crisis is not important merely because a major institution failed. It is important because it illustrates a recurring foreign-policy temptation: mistaking strategic or ideological alignment for evidence of democratic resilience.

The familiar bank-run scene in Capra’s film offers a useful point of comparison. Panic spreads, depositors demand their money, and George Bailey explains that the money is not sitting in a vault but invested throughout the community. The institution survives because people trust both the system and the people running it.

Paraguay’s crisis turned that premise on its head . The question many Paraguayans began asking was not merely where the money had gone. It was whether key institutions had come to serve a political elite rather than the public.

The problem was not simply that Washington missed warning signs. It was that many policymakers viewed Paraguay primarily through the lens of strategic and ideological alignment.

Paraguay’s standing in Washington rested on several factors. It remained one of Taiwan’s few diplomatic partners, maintained close relations with Israel , and increasingly aligned itself with influential conservative political movements in the United States. These attributes made Paraguay attractive as a geopolitical and ideological partner. But they also had an unintended consequence: governance concerns were increasingly overshadowed by other priorities. Evidence that would have prompted greater scrutiny elsewhere was often viewed through the assumption that a friendly government was also a healthy one.

The financial sector provided some of the clearest warning signs.

During Peña’s presidency, public funds increasingly flowed toward Ueno Bank, associated with Peña, and Banco Basa, long linked to Cartes. Government financial data showed an extraordinary concentration of public deposits and financial instruments in those institutions, while Paraguay’s social security system approved major purchases of Ueno bonds despite growing concerns about conflicts of interest. The developments prompted an obvious question: Why was the state directing so much public money toward institutions associated with the country’s most powerful political figures?

In October 2024, when a reporter asked Peña whether investments involving Ueno represented a conflict of interest, he angrily denounced the allegation as a “nefarious lie.” Nor were those concerns difficult to find in official U.S. assessments. The U.S. Department of State’s 2024 Investment Climate Statement warned that “unchecked corruption, impunity, and graft continue to hinder Paraguay’s economy.” Peña disputed the report, while senior Paraguayan officials dismissed it as inaccurate.

During this period, I observed a widening gap between how many Paraguayans understood their country’s trajectory and how it was often perceived in Washington. Conversations with journalists, civil-society leaders, businesspeople, and governance specialists frequently returned to concerns about the growing concentration of political and economic power around Cartes and his allies.

Among some policymakers and congressional observers in Washington, however, anti-corruption efforts were viewed less as responses to governance risks than as politically charged interventions . As a result, evidence of institutional deterioration was frequently filtered through ideological assumptions rather than evaluated on its own terms.

Yet Washington increasingly shifted attention away from governance concerns and toward geopolitical and ideological priorities. Sanctions were lifted , support for democracy and civil-society programs diminished, and anti-corruption efforts lost momentum. Whatever the rationale, the cumulative effect was to signal that institutional concerns were no longer paramount.

The collapse of Ueno finally exposed Paraguay’s crisis.

What appeared to be a banking scandal revealed a political system in which patronage networks, conflicts of interest, financial influence, and political authority had become deeply intertwined. The consequences were not abstract. Ueno’s failure left millions of customers unable to access their savings and disrupted payments and wages, while raising serious questions about the management of hundreds of millions of dollars in public deposits. For ordinary Paraguayans, the crisis was a deeply personal reminder of what happens when the institutions entrusted with protecting their financial security become entangled in political and economic power.

For years, Paraguayan cartoonists portrayed Peña as Cartes’ puppet. The caricature reflected a widely held perception that Peña’s political fortunes depended on the political machine Cartes built and continued to influence. When Cartes signaled support for Peña’s removal , the president’s political position unraveled with astonishing speed. Yet the larger lesson extends beyond any individual leader. The real issue was not the puppet but the system holding the strings.

Peña’s removal did not dismantle the machinery that had produced him. Pedro Alliana , who succeeded Peña as president, was one of Horacio Cartes’ closest political allies and had served as Peña’s vice president. Antonio Barrios , chosen to replace Alliana as vice president, had longstanding personal and political ties to Cartes. Although the transition altered the names at the top of the government, it did little to change perceptions that the same power structure remained firmly in place.

Paraguay matters not because it is unique but because it illustrates a temptation that recurs throughout American foreign policy. Policymakers naturally prefer partners who share their geopolitical priorities and ideological instincts. The danger comes when those affinities become substitutes for evaluating the strength of democratic institutions.

This is not just a Latin American story. Democracies rarely erode because leaders openly announce their intention to weaken institutions. More often, warning signs are rationalized away because the people benefiting from institutional decline are viewed as allies. Loyalty begins to outweigh accountability, and political convenience begins to outweigh democratic standards. By the time the consequences become impossible to ignore, many of the safeguards have already weakened.

Capra’s story endures because George Bailey reminds us that institutions are only as valuable as the communities they serve. Paraguay’s crisis tells the opposite story: what happens when institutions increasingly serve those who control them rather than the public that depends on them.

The dark sequel to It’s a Wonderful Life was never really about the bank. It was about the institutions behind it and the extent to which they had become vulnerable to political capture. Paraguay’s crisis should remind policymakers of a simple principle: strategic alignment and democratic resilience are not the same thing. When the former is allowed to obscure the latter, the consequences eventually become impossible to ignore.

stories.title: The Shenzhen Summit Supplants Yalta
stories.summary: The post The Shenzhen Summit Supplants Yalta appeared first on NOEMA .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
A world made safe for spheres of influence.

Nathan Gardels is the editor-in-chief of Noema Magazine. He is also the co-founder of and a senior adviser to the Berggruen Institute.

Pundits who dismissed the Shenzhen summit as a mere photo-op lacking substance missed the point. The significance of the conclave was precisely its enframing symbolism, showcasing a new world in which the rules-based order has been supplanted by spheres of influence accommodating each other.

The city of Shenzhen itself is a prism through which we can observe today’s power relations and the evolution of events over recent decades bringing us to this point.

Unplugged Computers in China’s Future Tech Hub

I first visited Shenzhen in 1986, arriving there by tram from Hong Kong and walking across the mainland border. There was barely any bustle, no crowds or traffic and a couple of tall buildings at the most. At our modest hotel, a squatting gardener was clipping the grass with a pair of scissors. The place still exuded the languorous vibe of the fishing village of 30,000 it had been not long before it was designated a “special economic zone” by Deng Xiaoping to attract foreign capital and technology.

On an inspection tour of sprouting industrial parks with then-former California governor Jerry Brown, our hosts proudly showed us what they called a tech hub. What then passed for “data centers” were cavernous, virtually empty warehouses with scores of desktop computers on worktables gathering dust — none were even plugged in.

What seemed embarrassing at the time turned out to be beyond impressive 40 years later. Shenzhen today is a literally glittering technopolis of 20 million people regarded as China’s “Silicon Valley” where Huawei, Tencent, DJI and BYD are all located. It is the center of gravity of China’s AI battle with the United States.

The invitation to visit had come some years earlier from Xi Zhongxun, then Party chief of Guangdong province (where Shenzhen is located) and the father of China’s current leader, Xi Jinping. The elder Xi had come to California in 1980 looking for investment in the special economic zone as a key platform of Deng’s policy of “reform and opening up” to the world. On that visit, he met Gov. Jerry Brown and toured the state, including stops at tech sites in the then-fledgling Silicon Valley (Apple and Intel were about it in those days) and Disneyland, where he gamely shook hands with Mickey Mouse.

Years later in 2012, when Brown was governor again for a second time, Xi Jinping, then-vice-president of China on his way to the top, visited California. The irony was not lost on either leader when the governor inquired whether China was interested in helping finance California’s bullet train, already in the works for nearly 20 years.

A Chinese delegation later met with the governor at the Peninsula Hotel in Beverly Hills to discuss possibilities, but the idea never panned out. Those who had once come cup in hand to the Golden State now offered financing terms too tough to abide. By 2026, China had built a 30,000-mile network of bullet trains spanning its vast country. California and the U.S. still have yet to build one.

On that 1986 trip to China, Brown and I also met at Zhongnanhai, the secluded leader’s compound in Beijing, with the ideology chief and youngest member of the ruling Communist Party Politburo at the time, Hu Qili. In a wide-ranging conversation that touched on topics from the “spiritual pollution” of Western influence to Tibetan Buddhism, Hu noted that the Chinese military had reduced its forces by one million soldiers. Many military installations, he said, were converting to commercial applications in light industry and heavy-truck production. Several military aircraft plants were now making refrigerators and motorcycles.

To this, Brown quipped, “If the army is making refrigerators, you must think the polar bear [what the Chinese called Russia] is hibernating.” Laughing, Hu simply replied that since Russia “couldn’t even consolidate control of Cambodia, it is only inviting great trouble to try anything with China.”

Opening then to America while hostile to an ebbing Soviet empire, Hu insisted that “China’s armed forces are sufficient to resist hegemonist efforts from the bear if they come.”

By the time I saw Hu again in 1988, Mikhail Gorbachev had come to power in the Kremlin, attracting some sympathy among reformers in China and inspiring a growing youth movement with his ideas of perestroika and glasnost. Enough of a thaw was in the works that Hu asked me to convey “fraternal greetings” to Aleksandr Yakovlev, then the Soviet party’s main reformist thinker, on my next stop in Moscow. Read Noema in print.

“The one key power left out of the 1945 Yalta talks that shaped the international order in the dying days of World War II is now setting the agenda for what comes next.”

The Tiananmen Turn

It was in that atmosphere that Gorbachev visited Beijing in May 1989 and met with Premier Zhao Ziyang as tensions with the authorities were mounting on Tiananmen Square. In the wake of the student massacre that June, the liberal-leaning Zhao was purged for revealing “state secrets” to Gorbachev by telling him that Deng, who would order the repression, remained the power behind the throne even though he had formally retired. Hu was also purged.

This was a “ludicrous accusation,” Gorbachev told me later. The real issue, as he saw it, was his advice that the student occupation should be defused politically through negotiation, not force. “I was confident a political solution could be found. I was wrong, unfortunately,” the last Soviet leader lamented.

Deng had drawn the line on Party control that Gorbachev was erasing in Moscow. Deng’s open palm on the economy clenched into an iron fist on political reform. Ever since, Gorbachev’s “new thinking” has been vilified in Beijing as a recipe for the collapse of the Party-state, and something to be avoided at all costs.

A World Safe For Spheres Of Influence

When Vladimir Putin emerged in the tumultuous years after the Soviet collapse, China’s sympathy with a more amenable Russia returned. As the post-Cold War years wore on, the “hegemonist threat” for China shifted to America, even as it prospered from the relationship.

In the end, China’s leaders came to strategically favor a trusted autocrat ruthlessly obsessed with dominating his own neighborhood over a meddling America endlessly endeavoring, in their minds, to subvert China’s governing system and keep the nation down. Party ideologues, Xi above all, are convinced that the American political class, implicitly if not explicitly, concurs with Bill Clinton’s remark when he was president that China was on “the wrong side of history.” Like many others in those days, Clinton wrongly presumed trade winds would blow open the society.

With a militarily mighty but economically feeble and dependent Russia at its side, China’s leaders have grown more confident in their capacity to contain America in a world made safe for spheres of influence.

The few words spoken for public consumption at the Shenzhen summit about zones of “civilizational values” and the primacy of state sovereignty over international law were code for the long-standing views of Xi and Putin, which the American president has now openly embraced.

Tech Trips The Thucydides Trap

At the first meeting of the Berggruen Institute’s 21st Century Council with Xi Jinping in 2013, the Party leader boasted that “we have never been closer to realizing the dream of Chinese rejuvenation” after the long climb back from colonial humiliation — invoking that history as if it were yesterday.

As Xi sees it, far from being on the wrong side of history, only the firm hand of the Communist Party could have brought the Middle Kingdom to where it is today and can take it where it must go tomorrow.

In 2015, then Premier Li Keqiang launched a “Made in China 2025” campaign with the goal of conquering the latest technologies from electric vehicles and batteries to artificial intelligence within a decade. Xi sees this conquest as rocket fuel for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, which he is determined to ensure does not fall behind the West and invite domination by outside forces, as it did during the Ming and Qing dynasties of the late 19th Century.

Strategists in Washington across the partisan landscape see China’s unrelenting resolve to reach its goals as an existential threat to America’s technological supremacy, and all that implies in terms of military might and geopolitical sway.

At our 2013 meeting, Xi pointedly raised an historical reference to “the Thucydides Trap,” whereby a rising power inevitably runs into conflict with an established power, only to say China would seek to avoid it. By now, though, it is clear that of all the contested issues between the U.S. and China, technology is most likely to trip the trap. The Nvidia episode is but one skirmish in a larger battle.

Shenzhen Supplants Yalta

If I were to have a conversation with the ideology chief on the Politburo today, as I had with Hu decades ago, here is what I would imagine him saying: “We have demonstrated we can go head-to-head with America on AI and technology. Today our military is reinvigorated. We have the largest navy in the world and are scaling up our nuclear arsenal toward parity with the U.S. and Russia. To be sure, America remains a formidable foe with the legacy of hegemonist ambitions. But let’s be serious. It is crumbling within. Its aging systems are plagued by outages. It can’t even build one bullet train.”

For Xi, hosting both leaders of the other great powers in Shenzhen, where China’s tech prowess is on full display, is the ultimate icing on the cake of rejuvenation. The one key power left out of the 1945 Yalta talks that shaped the international order in the dying days of World War II is now setting the agenda for what comes next.

stories.title: The Seduction of Donald Trump
stories.summary: Trump's quest to make his mark on the global stage threatens to be catastrophic. But it could be worse. The post The Seduction of Donald Trump appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin, and China's President Xi Jinping greet each other before the welcome banquet for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting at the Shenzhen International Communication Center on November 18, 2026 in Shenzhen, China (Iori Sagisawa-China Pool/Getty Images)

It was truly galling when Richard Nixon, the disgraced former U.S. president, became a respected elder statesman late in life. He published an embarrassment of a book on U.S.-Soviet relations in 1980—that nonetheless influenced incoming president Ronald Reagan. He traveled to Beijing after the Tiananmen Square massacre of 1989 in order to revive U.S.-Chinese relations by emphasizing commerce over morality. He had the ear of presidents from Ford to Clinton, which buoyed his reputation for geopolitical acuity even if what he had to say was just regurgitated realism.

Donald Trump has suffered a lifetime of disgraces—multiple bankruptcies, a gazillion lawsuits, a felony conviction, two impeachments, an election loss in 2020, and, earlier this month, a midterm repudiation. The cumulative effect of these public failures would prompt ordinary people to change their names, endure cosmetic surgery, and relocate to an obscure corner of the globe.

But shameless politicos, like Nixon and Trump, are always looking to regain the spotlight. Unlike Nixon, Trump did not try to resurrect his reputation as a post-presidential hobby. Instead he regained the Oval Office in 2024 largely to prove that he was right all along, despite all these setbacks. Over the last two years, he hasn’t made his case for redemption through arguments or by setting positive examples. Instead, he has focused on lying, bullying, and going after his enemies.

The next two years will include all of that, of course, but Trump is also likely to take a page from Nixon’s book by making his mark on international affairs. By this I don’t mean a fling with a Slovenian supermodel, though this is basically the sum total of Trump’s pre-presidential experience with foreign policy.

Trump has wanted to acquire the title of “elder statesman” ever since he returned to the Oval Office. Bagging a Nobel Peace Prize would have been an effective shortcut to this goal. To bolster his case for the prize, he has made bold claims about ending wars and heading off conflicts. By punishing bad guys—Maduro, Khamenei—he effectively styles himself as the ultimate good guy. The superpowers that he deploys—the Massive Ordnance Air Blast, the tariff, the sanction, the insult—all support his boast that he is righting historic wrongs.

In his final two years in office, Trump won’t be able to do much on the home front, thanks to a confrontational Congress. Instead, he will try to burnish—at least in his own mind—his foreign policy credentials. He will do so not through the conventional route of promoting democracy or making grand humanitarian gestures. Rather, he will stay within his comfort zone by focusing on making backroom deals with fellow strongmen.

The first stop on his two-year swan song of a world tour will be this week in Shenzhen, China.

The Troika

Once again channeling Nixon, Donald Trump wants to do something big on nuclear weapons. For Nixon, arms control negotiations were an opportunity to manage risk with the Soviet Union and, through the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, preserve the hegemonic power of the nuclear club, primarily the United States.

Trump, by contrast, doesn’t seem quite sure what he thinks about nuclear weapons.

The president has insisted that the United States has fallen behind in the nuclear race and must regain its number one position. Toward that end, the Trump administration has proposed a dramatic increase in spending on nuclear weapons to $71 billion as part of the $1.5 trillion defense budget. Over 30 years, the nuclear modernization program will cost $1.7 trillion . This is money spent, of course, on deterrence. But the president has also, from time to time, hinted at the use of nuclear weapons, most recently with his threats to annihilate Iran .

At the same time, Trump has talked about the importance of reaching nuclear arms control agreements with Russia and China. “There’s no reason for us to be building brand new nuclear weapons, we already have so many,” he said back in February 2025 , shortly after taking office. “You could destroy the world 50 times over, 100 times over. And here we are building new nuclear weapons, and they’re building nuclear weapons.”

That perhaps is the definition of world leader: someone who loudly laments all the money wasted on dangerous nuclear weapons even as they allocate even more funds to modernize the arsenal.

In any case, Trump is in China this week to cajole Putin and Xi into agreeing to something related to nuclear weapons. It’s going to be a heavy lift. Given the gap in size in the respective arsenals, China doesn’t believe that it has enough weapons to justify any limits. And Russia is in no mood to negotiate these days, despite the economic challenges it faces as a result of the war in Ukraine.

Actually, Trump has a lousy record when it comes to arms control. He tried to get trilateral discussions started in his first term but failed to extend the one major agreement with Russia, New START (which Biden ultimately secured). Then, in this term, Trump failed again to deal with a Russian proposal to limit deployment of nuclear weapons.

But nukes are not only thing on Trump’s mind.

A New Yalta?

Near the end of World War II, Franklin Delano Roosevelt met with Stalin and Winston Churchill at Yalta to discuss the post-war order. On the agenda was the future of Germany and Japan, the borders in and around Eastern Europe, the question of reparations, and the shape and functions of the United Nations.

Such a meeting of winners surely appeals to Trump, who wants only to sit at the big boy’s table since everything else is too low stakes for a superhero like himself. So, for instance, Trump arrived at this week’s meeting of Southeast Asian leaders so late that he could do little more than pose in the group photo. He has no interest in the United Nations, which he views solely as a once-a-year opportunity to hector the international community. He has experimented with his Board of Peace, which has barely had any effect in Gaza much less address other global problems.

Trump has put more emphasis on face-to-face meetings with Putin and Xi, though such bilateral negotiations have not yielded much either. He met Putin in Alaska last year and has conducted three sessions with Xi. The meeting with the Russian leader was all pomp and no circumstance. A few deals were concluded with Xi but nothing groundbreaking.

But a president can still dream. And Trump imagines that in Shenzhen he can put his name on a new security order in Europe, a superpower agreement on non-proliferation, perhaps even a roadmap for peace in the Middle East. All that’s required is a bit of autocrat-wrangling, which Trump prides himself on being an expert.

But the only person likely to be wrangled in Shenzhen is Trump himself. He has revealed a keen ability to be snowed by Putin, who has nimbly avoided additional sanctions and won various favors from the Trump administration in exchange for…what? The Russian leader has proven worse than uncompromising in negotiations around the war in Ukraine, most recently in Abu Dhabi where he insisted that NATO return to its pre-1997 deployments .

Instead of offering to compromise on Ukraine—on territory or security guarantees or even ceasefires—Putin is offering Trump something much dearer to the U.S. president’s heart: access to Russian fossil fuel riches.

According to The New York Times , Russia has been offering to sell off Lukoil assets—oil fields, refineries, gas stations—to a close Trump ally (Todd Boehly), two Gulf investors with ties to Jared Kushner (Moutaz and Ramez Al-Khayyat), and an Emirati royal connected to Steve Witkoff (Sheikh Tahnoon). The U.S. International Development Finance Corporation would also get a piece of the action. Corruption, which was a top issue in the U.S. midterm elections , continues to be a guiding principle of policymaking in the Trump administration.

China has seduced Trump in a different way. It fell back on a more traditional honeypot scheme to ensnare Trump’s key computer chip ally, Jensen Huang of Nvidia. It just so happens that Nvidia is the only company that produces the chips necessary for the most powerful AI applications. And it just so happens that Huang, who was having an affair with a reputed Chinese spy, was lobbying Trump to send more of those chips to China.

Such traditional spycraft aside, China has been content to stand back and benefit from Trump’s self-inflicted wounds—the disastrous war with Iran, the tariffs against allies and adversaries, and the withdrawal from international agreements and institutions. Perhaps Trump is only accelerating U.S. decline, but China is grateful nonetheless for the revised timeline.

Putin wants to play Trump. China is happy to let Trump be Trump. They both relish the opportunity in Shenzhen to feed Trump’s delusions of grandeur. They’ll give the U.S. president a stage on which he can strut as an elder statesman. They’ll give him compliments.

But they won’t give him any real agreements.

The Next Two Years

Nixon was loathsome, to be sure, but he wasn’t stupid. Tutored by Henry Kissinger, the former president at least understood the basics of geopolitics. Also, his attempt to launder his reputation was basically harmless, at least compared to the war crimes he committed as president.

Trump, on the other hand, can do immense damage in his last two years in office. Blocked by Congress from doing more DOGE-like damage to the U.S. government, he will turn his attention to furthering his campaign to destroy international institutions. The war the administration has launched against the International Criminal Court will serve as a model.

The seduction of Trump by Putin and Xi—along with lesser autocrats like Modi, Erdogan, and Milei—could have even more damaging consequences. Putin will wield Trump like a machete to cut the strings that hold together NATO and the European Union. China will use Trump’s anti-internationalism to remake global affairs in its own image—mercantile, extractivist, autocratic. Trump, seduced, will think that he is at the helm, an elder statesman coming into his own, putting his mark on the world much as he is making his mark on Washington, DC.

With Trump, this might be the best-case scenario. The alternative—increased conflict with Russia or China or both—would be even more catastrophic. Yes, it’s a horrifying prospect, but let Trump believe that he is remaking the world.

It’s better than his unmaking of it.

stories.title: Russia, India, and Saudi Arabia Are Stalling a Key U.N. Climate Report
stories.summary: Experts are warning that political attacks on a critical scientific report could undermine the basis for future U.N. climate negotiations. Read more on E360 →
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
This article was originally published by Inside Climate News and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

A coal mine in Jharkhand, India. Vishal Kumar Singh / AFP via Getty Images via Inside Climate News

Experts are warning that political attacks on a critical scientific report could undermine the basis for future U.N. climate negotiations.

The science that guides negotiators and policymakers at the United Nations’ COP31 climate change conference is “under a serious and highly politicized attack,” said Laurence Tubiana, a veteran French climate diplomat and one of the architects of the 2015 Paris climate agreement.

The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, established in 1988 to inform international climate negotiations, regularly assesses thousands of studies on rising temperatures, sea level rise, melting ice, and strategies for adapting to the increasingly intense impacts of global warming.

But three countries — Russia and Saudi Arabia, both major fossil fuel producers, and India, which accounts for an estimated 14 percent of global coal consumption — are blocking progress on future reports, according to scientists on the panel and independent observers.

Those countries “are doing everything they can to slow the process,” Tubiana said. They are becoming less discreet about their efforts, she said, as they increasingly view their economies as threatened by a conditional agreement to transition away from coal, oil, and gas reached during COP28, the 2023 Conference of the Parties in Dubai.

The science panel’s current impasse is especially troubling, “because we know climate problems are accelerating, and we need a lot of data and communication to understand what’s happening at this COP,” said Mary Robinson, former president of Ireland and former United Nations special envoy on climate change.

Robinson said this isn’t the first time countries have tried to obstruct science. Recent examples include attacks seeking to undermine a recent United Nations Environment Programme report on “overshoot,” which concludes that there is no way to avoid passing the 1.5 degree C warming target in the Paris Agreement.

Fossil fuels account for an estimated 80 percent to 90 percent of planet-heating carbon dioxide emissions, according to the IPCC’s 2023 assessment .

The international climate science panel relies on voluntary donations from member countries to fund its work, including periodic assessments, some of which inform steps required under the Paris Agreement. The panel has yet to set a budget for next year, potentially delaying a scientific report needed ahead of next year’s U.N. climate conference.

“Since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the oil and gas sector has become much more aggressive,” Tubiana said. “I think this is partly because it sees its dominance over energy starting to erode.”

Oil and gas companies are losing ground in transport as electric-vehicle adoption in Asia surges faster than expected, she said, adding that reports from the International Energy Agency show demand for fossil fuels is set to slow.

“Investors hear the message that the decline is coming, and those governments have pushed back,” she said.

The 2023 IPCC report concluded that existing and planned fossil fuel infrastructure would push global warming beyond the Paris Agreement goal of limiting warming as close as possible to 1.5 degrees C above the preindustrial average.

Tubiana said a growing number of countries view the transition away from fossil fuels as a path to greater energy independence and security, while those opposed to the shift are becoming “more angry and vocal.”

“The danger,” she said, “is that they take other countries along with them that aren’t necessarily committed to that position.”

The latest draft of the conference’s decision document highlights the assessments’ importance to the negotiations. Some countries also want to include language that could help break the science panel’s deadlock, but the same countries stalling the IPCC are resisting that effort.

In particular, the climate, environment, and energy ministers participating in the current round of talks could help the IPCC get over the political hurdles it faces, said Bill Hare, CEO of Climate Analytics, an international climate science and policy institute.

Hare said the countries participating in the U.N. talks should advocate for continued support for the IPCC. If the panel can’t deliver the needed climate science “because of political obstacles created by a small number of countries, it would be a historic setback for the connection between science and the international climate process.”

Robinson said some of the world’s least developed countries and small island states “desperately need” the international panel’s reports because they can’t do their own climate assessments.

“We need the authoritative, legitimate IPCC science, which has guided us from the beginning in this whole climate process,” she said. “It’s just a sign of the difficult times we’re in that we have to fight for it. I can hardly believe it.”

— Bob Berwyn , Inside Climate News

stories.body:
Regulation alone won’t fix the conditions that have earned China the reputation of the “Wild East.”

Jane Qiu is an independent science writer in Beijing.

BEIJING — In March 2023, four-year-old Mei in Shanghai was diagnosed with a rare genetic mutation linked to developmental delay and autism-like traits. Although her condition was mild and she improved with therapy and special education, her parents remained worried about her future. Hopeful for a cure, they paid Qiu Zilong, a renowned neuroscientist at Shanghai Jiao Tong University, and his team $860,000 to develop a customized gene therapy. The treatment, which used adeno-associated viruses to deliver gene editors to the brain, had been approved by Xinhua Hospital, a leading hospital for rare diseases.

On March 24, 2025, trillions of viral particles carrying gene editors were injected into Mei’s spinal cord. She soon developed a fever and kidney failure and died within days. A year later, Qiu’s team published its preclinical findings in Nature. Mei’s case was hailed by Chinese media as “a world-class breakthrough.” Mei’s death and her family’s financial support were not mentioned.

Deaths in clinical trials are not unusual. What is shocking are the regulatory lapses revealed by an investigation published this July in Science and subsequently corroborated by a separate investigation conducted by the Shanghai municipal government, which released its findings last week. The treatment’s consent form, for instance, didn’t warn of the possibility of death. The hospital had approved treatment before toxicology findings showing liver and kidney damage in monkeys that received similar treatments. And, among other crucial omissions, the researchers failed to disclose Mei’s death.

Apparently, this was not an isolated incident. Several researchers told me that Chinese hospitals commonly fail to disclose adverse events. On Aug. 5, STAT reported another death in a gene-editing trial led by Shanghai-based HuidaGene, an incident that had remained undisclosed for about 15 months. (The Chinese team published their findings , including the fatal case, in Cell on Oct. 26.) A founder of a rare-disease organization in China told me, on condition of anonymity for fear of political repercussions, that she had encountered other trials for genetic disorders in which deaths had gone unreported. Recent revelations of undisclosed deaths in clinical trials conducted in China have prompted warnings against the use of Chinese data in U.S. drug development.

As someone who has reported on China’s ethical governance for two decades, this all feels like déjà vu. Since modern bioethics was introduced to China in the late 1980s, its history has been punctuated by one scandal after another — often fueled by hype surrounding emerging technologies — that have earned the country a reputation as biotechnology’s “Wild East.”

Back in 2006, patients flocked to China to receive unproven stem-cell therapies . When immunotherapies came into vogue a decade later, bogus advertisements for unproven interventions proliferated online until the health ministry stepped in after the high-profile death of 21-year-old student Wei Zexi. Two years later, biophysicist He Jiankui shocked the world by announcing the birth of the first genetically modified babies created using CRISPR technology.

The response in China to Mei’s death has been divided. Some netizens portray Qiu as a reckless scientist willing to gamble with patients’ lives. Others, including longtime acquaintances, describe him as a diligent scientist committed to helping patients. In some respects, Qiu represents the antithesis of He. After the CRISPR-babies scandal, Qiu openly condemned He’s reckless behavior — only to become embroiled in a comparable scandal himself six years later.

It might be tempting to blame such scandals on individual failings. The deeper questions are: What systemic factors shaped their behavior? What does the incident reveal about China’s Achilles heel in biotechnology—and about the broader culture of international science in which it is embedded? And what can the lessons teach clinical research worldwide?

Fatal Flaw

It would be unfair to suggest that China hasn’t tried to strengthen its ethical governance. The CRISPR-babies scandal prompted deep soul-searching among Chinese scholars and government officials. Since then, President Xi Jinping reportedly championed an “ethics first” approach, contrasting the “science first” mindset often seen in Chinese research. New measures have included incorporating ethics provisions in China’s first Civil Law Code, creating a national ethics committee , and enacting new ethics-review guidelines for clinical research.

But powerful forces are also pushing in the opposite direction. In 2016, China launched Healthy China 2030, making rapid application of emerging medical technologies in clinical practice a priority — not only to address unmet medical needs but to boost national competitiveness. Reforms created a new pathway to translate basic research into clinical applications for cutting-edge technologies overseen by the health ministry, alongside the conventional drug-approval route regulated by the National Medical Products Administration (NMPA), China’s equivalent of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). This became widely known as the dual-track regulatory system.

“Since modern bioethics was introduced to China in the late 1980s, its history has been punctuated by one scandal after another — often fueled by hype surrounding emerging technologies.”

Under the technology track, clinical trials are often initiated by university researchers working with hospital clinicians rather than companies. Such investigator-initiated trials (IITs) exist worldwide. Until new regulations took effect this May, Chinese IITs were distinctive in that they could proceed with hospital approvals without the national regulatory oversight required for conventional drug trials. Compared with the NMPA route, the faster pathway allowed researchers to assess promising technologies in humans more quickly and at lower costs and help attract investment.

The result was a boom in IITs. By one estimate , more than 40,000 had been registered by April 2026, involving hundreds of thousands of participants and accounting for much of China’s translational research aimed at applying basic research to clinical practice.

China’s IIT model attracted worldwide attention. Kiran Musunuru, an expert on gene therapy at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, told me that “there is a widespread perception” that Chinese-style IITs offer a way to conduct first-in-human trials quickly and inexpensively. U.S. companies are increasingly interested in conducting IITs in China. Some U.S. researchers have even argued that the U.S should adopt elements of China’s model to accelerate drug discovery and enhance its competitiveness.

Critics, however, point to a fatal flaw: quality control. Driven by the pursuit of high-impact papers— whether for career advancement or hospital rankings — researchers rushed into first-in-human trials of emerging technologies. Hospitals are overwhelmed by proposals involving technologies with varying levels of risk. Researchers told me that as many as two dozen applications can be assessed in a single afternoon. In many cases, the process has become “a rubber-stamping exercise,” explained Zhu Wei, a bioethicist at the Shanghai Clinical Research Center.

A recent analysis of Chinese stem-cell IITs found that although a small fraction helped accelerate the application of basic research to clinical practice, most were repetitive, lacked innovation and wasted resources. Musunuru — who led the landmark development of a personalized gene-editing trial for Baby KJ, an infant with a rare life-threatening deficiency of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 that can cause dangerous ammonia buildup in the blood — warns that allowing individual hospitals to approve first-in-human trials of emerging technologies is particularly dangerous, because few researchers have sufficient experience to assess their risks. They would be “operating blind,” he told me, leaving the outcome dependent on “their appetite for risk.” That appetite can be amplified by institutional conflicts of interest. Successful trials of emerging technologies can bring researchers and hospitals fame, career advancement, high rankings and resources. Jing-Bao Nie, a bioethicist at the University of Otago in Dunedin, New Zealand, told me that these incentives can undermine institutional judgment and jeopardize patient safety. In Mei’s case, he noted, the lure of a “world-class breakthrough” may have overwhelmed necessary caution. Political interference, which is common in China, is another way the appetite for risk may outweigh caution. Chinese researchers told me that senior hospital leaders often chair the committees that review trial applications. When they seek to push through major projects led by prominent scientists, other committee members may feel unable to object. Read Noema in print. A central regulator is more insulated from such pressures and can also draw on a far broader pool of expertise. As Musumuru notes, the FDA has an army of experienced reviewers who have assessed successful and failed trials, as well as those involving serious adverse effects. Its decisions are therefore informed by “the widest possible body of knowledge,” he told me. “That’s very reassuring.” Oversight Deficiencies Zhai Xiaomei, a bioethicist at the Peking Union Medical College and a member of the national science and technology ethics committee, was not wrong when she told New Beijing News that the problems exposed by Mei’s tragedy had improved since China’s State Council Order No. 818, which established a new regulatory framework for clinical research and commercial application of cutting-edge biomedical technologies, took effect this May. Under the new rules, only top-tier hospitals can undertake IITs. Trials involving emerging technologies like gene and cell therapy, brain-machine interfaces, transplantation and microbial therapies must undergo further review by the health ministry after hospital approval. Adverse effects must be reported within five working days. Violations can result in fines, suspension or permanent ban on clinical research, loss of licenses and even criminal charges. The scientific community in China and abroad welcomes the new rules. But a researcher working closely with the ministry, who spoke on condition of anonymity due to potential career repercussions, told me that it lacks sufficient staff with the necessary technical expertise to review the large volume of applications. Consequently, the researcher added, the reviews rely heavily on experts from universities and hospitals, with only a handful assessing each case. By contrast, Musunuru told me that the U.S. FDA employs numerous in-house reviewers, many with decades of experience, and dozens pore over each submission. If translating emerging technologies into clinical practice remains a national priority, he argues, China must make sustained investments in regulatory expertise to ensure trial safety and quality. “If translating emerging technologies into clinical practice remains a national priority, China must make sustained investments in regulatory expertise to ensure trial safety and quality.” More troublingly, Order 818 lacks mechanisms to monitor what happens locally and identify violations. It includes neither an inspection process — a crucial component of regulatory oversight in countries such as the U.S. and UK — nor a whistleblowing platform for reporting adverse effects and deaths. Such mechanisms are particularly important in countries where transparency is limited, and the press is not free. Without them, violations may go unnoticed and the penalties risk becoming little more than empty threats. Researchers, like bioethicist Ma Yonghui of Xiamen University, also worry that regulatory exemptions could create loopholes. Military hospitals, for instance, fall outside health ministry rules. The two dozen or so free trade zones across China, particularly in Bo’ao on the tropical island of Hainan, may enjoy special regulatory treatment, potentially attracting foreign researchers and companies seeking to conduct ethically contentious trials they could not undertake in their own countries. There are ample precedents of scientists exploiting countries with weak ethics governance as sites for risky research. In October 2018, one month before the CRISPR-babies scandal, He and John Zhang, founder and medical director of the New Hope Fertility Center in New York City, met Hainan’s vice governor to discuss establishing a clinic in Bo’ao to offer experimental procedures, including heritable genome editing. Zhang had already attracted international attention in 2016 for helping produce in Mexico the world’s first “three-parent baby” to prevent the transmission of mitochondrial DNA mutations from the mother. The procedure involved replacing faulty mitochondria with healthy ones from a female donor during in vitro fertilization, a procedure that was — and still is — illegal in the U.S. Hype & Hope While Mei’s death has prompted renewed soul-searching over China’s ethical failings, it would be a mistake to see it simply as a scientific scandal that can be fixed with new regulations, Nie told me. The case offers a window into people’s relationship with biotechnology in China as well as their hopes and expectations — shaped not only by scientists but by society at large. Over the past decade, rare-disease advocacy organizations have grown rapidly in China, helping improve patient care, pressing for government support and driving research through collecting genetic data, studying disease progression and funding clinical trials. Su Yeyang, an independent anthropologist in Langfang in Hebei province who works with rare-disease communities, told me this has given families a sense of agency. With limited social support and a market-driven drug-discovery model that has failed rare-disease communities worldwide, they are doing whatever they can “to help themselves, their children and their community,” she said. With gene therapy, the “magic cure” long hoped for by many rare-disease patients seems within reach. In one high-profile case, a fledgling company approached Xu Wei, a high-school graduate in his 30s in Kunming, in China’s southern province of Yunnan, to develop a gene therapy for his son. The boy had Menkes syndrome, a rare genetic disorder that impairs copper absorption and causes developmental delays and premature death. The company, with no track record in neurodevelopmental diseases, claimed to have developed the treatment in less than a year. In 2022, the 3-year-old received it at a private hospital in a trial that, based on publicly available accounts, appeared not to include biomarker or behavioral assessments of efficacy. Chinese media reported enthusiastically on anecdotal claims of improvements while downplaying the risks of undertaking such experimental therapies. A patient advocacy leader told me such cases are not uncommon in China, where at least 20 million people are living with rare diseases. They offer hope, whether grounded in evidence or not, and can encourage others to follow. “We try to explain to families that pouring millions into a trial is no guarantee of success” and could even backfire, she says. Even well-educated parents, like Mei’s, may underestimate the complexity of clinical research and overestimate what experimental therapies can achieve. It’s unclear whether Qiu, who was fired by the university last week and barred from participating in scientific research for five years following the government investigation , helped foster such expectations. He has not publicly given his account. But his book, “ The Autism Enlightenment ,” published this April, was revealing. It recounted how, in 2010, he told the mother of a child with Rett syndrome — a rare, genetic neurodevelopmental disorder leading to severe cognitive and physical impairments — that a cure would likely emerge in three to five years. It did not discuss fatal risks often associated with first-in-human trials. It did not mention Jessie Gelsinger, who had a mild form of ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, a condition that can lead to abnormally high levels of ammonia in the blood and died in 1999 from a preventable complication of an experimental gene therapy. “While Mei’s death has prompted renewed soul-searching over China’s ethical failings, it would be a mistake to see it simply as a scientific scandal that can be fixed with new regulations.” Gelsinger was the first person publicly identified as having died in a gene therapy clinical trial, which undermined public trust in the field and set back its progress for decades. Nor did the book draw caution from the death in 2024 of a girl with Rett syndrome in the first brain-directed gene therapy for the condition. In both cases, scientists used the same type of virus as Qiu did. In a society where disability and genetic disease remain stigmatized, and families receive limited support, Mei’s parents placed their hopes in Qiu and gene editing. Like the couple who turned to He Jiankui to protect their children from HIV and the associated discrimination by editing their embryos, they sought a technological solution to social problems. As the Illness Challenge Foundation, a Beijing-based rare-disease advocacy organization, put it after Mei’s death , “responsible innovation should not entice patients to stake their lives in the name of hope.” China’s Gelsinger Moment? Gelsinger’s death in 1999 was a game changer. It’s widely regarded as a cautionary tale of how a toxic combination of scientific hype and insufficient safeguards can jeopardize patient safety. It triggered institutional reforms and significant changes in research culture in the U.S. that were aimed at rebuilding public and regulatory trust. Mei’s death could be China’s Gelsinger moment. It has exposed regulatory failings, a scientific ethos that encourages hype and recklessness, and deeper societal problems surrounding disability and genetic disease. None is unique to China, but they are particularly acute in a country facing a distinctive combination of political and developmental challenges. At the heart of the incident lies the “moral arbitrage” of experimental therapies, a recurrent theme in biotechnological innovation worldwide. On one hand, patients want access to cutting-edge, unproven treatments when they see them as their only hope. On the other hand, such treatments carry risks, which often accompany medical breakthroughs. Navigating the contours between hope and risk requires more than scientific evidence and regulatory rules, Su told me. It demands critical reflection on the culture of international science that places a premium on competition, sensational research, and being first at any cost. It also calls for broader societal dialogues about the diverse notions of human flourishing, the stigmatization of disabilities, and the need for greater support for people living with rare diseases. If China can learn from the failures and undertake the regulatory, scientific and social reforms needed to address its biotech governance failures — and if the rest of the world can look beyond the country’s small number of success stories out of a hidden ocean of low-quality and potentially harmful clinical trials — Mei’s death will not have been in vain. stories.body:
A Catholic priest offers a blessing on the shores of Lake Victoria. Priests perform rituals at landing sites, praying for bountiful catches at an increasingly unpredictable time.

PHOTO ESSAY

The largest tropical lake on Earth, Africa’s Lake Victoria is under enormous strain, with its waters contaminated, fisheries decimated, and shorelines drowning. The losses have spurred renewed calls to protect the lake, which supports more than 45 million people across the region.

By Matilde Gattoni and Matteo Fagotto • November 19, 2026

Facebook

Twitter

LinkedIn

Email

Lake Victoria, the largest tropical lake on Earth, is under enormous strain as overfishing, pollution, and a changing climate are decimating its fisheries, contaminating its waters, and bringing record floods to its shores. The losses have spurred renewed calls to protect the lake, whose basin supports more than 45 million people across the region.

For decades, Lake Victoria’s fishing industry relied on bountiful catches of Nile tilapia and Nile perch, both introduced to the lake in the 1950s. The perch, a voracious predator blamed for the disappearance of some 200 native cichlid species, became the lake’s most lucrative prize, with its filets exported to Europe and the Middle East. In recent years, overfishing has dramatically reduced fish stocks, including perch, pushing many fishermen to use illegal fine-mesh nets that catch juvenile fish before they can reproduce. Kenya’s catch fell from 94,349 metric tons in 2021 to 70,231 metric tons in 2025, according to the country’s fisheries service. In Uganda, the number of plants processing Nile perch has dropped from 21 to six, according to the director of operations at Victoria Treasures, one of the few surviving factories.

Pollution from farms, gold mining, and booming shoreline cities — including Kampala, Uganda’s capital, and Mwanza, Tanzania’s second-largest city — has compounded the damage as untreated sewage and fertilizers feed recurring algal blooms and water hyacinth invasions, which starve the water of oxygen and suffocate fish.

Yale Environment 360 / Created with Datawrapper

Making matters worse, exceptional rains linked with climate change lifted the lake to record levels in 2020 and again in 2024. The floods have forced hundreds of thousands of people from their homes and swallowed farmland and fish landing sites. The World Meteorological Organization expects this year’s El Niño, which typically brings heavier rains to East Africa, to last into 2027, raising the risk of further displacement.

In July, during the UNESCO World Heritage Committee meeting in Busan, South Korea, more than 100 civil society groups from 35 countries proposed recognizing Lake Victoria as a living cultural landscape, based on the fishing knowledge, rituals, and oral traditions its lakeside communities have accumulated over generations. The groups insisted that any nomination should protect local communities from displacement and safeguard the livelihoods of both fishers and the women who sell their catch.

If approved, inscription on the World Heritage list could bring international attention, technical help, and limited funding. It would also commit the governments of Kenya, Uganda, and Tanzania to protecting the lake under an agreed management plan.

Photographer Matilde Gattoni spent February and March on Lake Victoria’s Kenyan, Ugandan, and Tanzanian shores. This photo essay combines images that reflect the lake’s dire condition — from the water hyacinths that clog landing sites to the residents displaced by floods — with images that speak to the countless ties, both economic and spiritual, that continue to bind the people to the lake.

Scroll down to see the images, or click on the photo below to launch a slideshow.

Invasive water hyacinth in Ogenya, Kenya, robs the lake of dissolved oxygen and blocks sunlight from penetrating the water. The weed, pushed by the wind into shallow areas, also keeps fishermen from reaching open water.

In Sindo, Kenya, women working as fishmongers vie for a piece of a dwindling catch. The competition has led to jaboya , or “sex for fish”: Women must trade sexual favors with fishermen to secure enough product to provide for their families.

Joyce Akinyi Odiko, 53, began as a fish seller but eventually assembled her own fleet of 30 boats, becoming one of the few women on the lake to own what she catches. As fisheries collapse in Uhanya, Kenya, she is considering selling her boats and leaving fishing behind.

A trader sells omena and fried fish in the largest market in Kisumu, Kenya. Populations of omena have plummeted as a result of overfishing and warming that is reducing oxygen levels in the lake.

A young woman in Uhanya, Kenya, wades through the submerged ruins of a communal fish processing site. In many coastal villages, floods have swallowed infrastructure, displaced residents, and moved the shoreline hundreds of feet inland.

Rising lake levels destroyed the mud and log home of Jane Anyango Okelo, in Ogenya. When the water receded it left behind highly fertile soil for crops, but Jane and her husband can’t afford to rebuild their home and now live in a makeshift tent.

A girl eats her only meal of the day in an alley of the informal camp at the Kigungu landing site in Uganda. Most of the people here are refugees from Makusa and Lwamunyo islands, which were almost entirely submerged by floods in 2020.

Many fishermen have turned to sand mining in nearby river mouths as fish stocks have shrunk. The practice is illegal as dredging destroys vital fish breeding grounds, disturbs the habitats of hippos and crocodiles, and leads to the erosion of wetlands.

A laborer carries a massive bundle of rice hay on his back after the harvest in Nduru, Kenya. Fertilizer runoff from farms in the region flows directly into the nearby Nyando River and into Lake Victoria, fueling the growth of invasive water hyacinth that chokes the shoreline.

Mercury used in informal and largely unregulated gold mining operations in Macalder, Kenya, can spill into rivers that eventually discharge into Lake Victoria.

A young girl in Kigungu examines a freshly caught Nile perch. Stocks of the highly profitable fish have dwindled, so processing companies now hire agents to scour landing sites and rush large specimens to factories for export.
