stories.body:
Billionaire commerce secretary faces scrutiny after sex scandal reveals his role in sales of chips to China

Howard Lutnick, the beleaguered US commerce secretary and close ally of Donald Trump , is emerging as Democrats’ prime target when the party takes control of Congress in January.

Lutnick is resisting calls to resign amid a bipartisan outcry over his role in the scandal at artificial intelligence (AI) company Nvidia and the sale of microchips to China , the US’s principal geopolitical rival in the race for AI supremacy.

The 65-year-old billionaire received a vote of confidence from Trump on Friday but faces growing criticism from some Republicans and a chorus of Democrats vowing to investigate his actions and demanding that he testify on Capitol Hill. Among their questions is whether Lutnick compromised national security to make money for his family.

Although cabinet members such as the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, and the health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, have faced calls for accountability, Lutnick is now in the sights of a newly emboldened Congress eager to bring the Trump administration to book .

“To this point he has been overshadowed by some of the more controversial characters in the Trump administration,” said Kurt Bardella , an adviser to Democrats in Texas and former congressional aide. “It wasn’t until a scandal that literally has everything from spies to China to sex to a billionaire CEO that the commerce secretary got on the radar of the entire political and media apparatus.”

Lutnick’s friendship with Trump was forged decades ago in New York’s business world and deepened after Trump supported Lutnick as he rebuilt Cantor Fitzgerald following the 11 September 2001 attacks. Lutnick later became one of Trump’s most prominent corporate backers, helping bankroll his political comeback and co-chairing his 2024 transition team.

But his position is under threat after Nvidia co-founder and chief executive Jensen Huang was forced to resign over an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International who is suspected by US intelligence agencies of being a Chinese spy.

Megaspeed allegedly served as a conduit for the diversion of $4bn in advanced Nvidia AI semiconductors to Chinese technology firms, in breach of US export controls.

A public dispute erupted between Lutnick and the treasury secretary, Scott Bessent , who revealed that the treasury, defense and state departments, as well as the US trade representative, had wanted to put Megaspeed on a trade blacklist months earlier, only for Lutnick’s commerce department to stall enforcement.

Bessent said, “Commerce has the pen, and you will have to ask them about their internal processes,” adding that his deputy had pushed the issue for months.

That leaves Lutnick vulnerable to the charge that he either personally intervened or instructed subordinates to disregard intelligence warnings and allow the chip sales to continue. He is facing a rare backlash from both sides of the aisle.

Republican Tom Cotton, who chairs the Senate intelligence committee, told ‌the Wall Street Journal that Lutnick repeatedly ignored warnings that AI chips were ‌being smuggled to China before the Nvidia scandal became public. Lutnick should have taken “the threats of communist China more seriously”, Cotton said.

John Kennedy of Louisiana, another Republican and a member of the Senate banking committee, urged Lutnick to hold a press conference to explain what he knew. He said: “The commerce department greenlit $4bn of sales of advanced chips to the company of the spy that Mr Huang was having an affair with and I want to know why.”

The Republican senator Tim Scott, of South Carolina, has written to Lutnick and Huang requesting their testimony in front of the Senate banking committee next month. Scott wrote on social media: “Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology.”

Democrats are queueing up with further investigations once they take power in January.

The Oregon senator Ron Wyden and the Massachusetts congressman Richard Neal, the top Democrats on the Senate finance and House ways and means committees, respectively, have written to Lutnick demanding that he preserve all records related to decisions about Nvidia chip exports, pending an investigation.

Trump’s approval of advanced Nvidia chip exports to China “raises critical questions about whether and to what extent political considerations are improperly influencing policy decisions made by the administration”, Wyden and Neal wrote .

Meanwhile, the representatives Jamie Raskin of Maryland, Gregory Meeks of New York and Sydney Kamlager-Dove of California have launched an inquiry into whether Lutnick used his office to help Cantor Fitzgerald, now controlled by his sons, avoid losses connected to scrutiny of Nvidia.

after newsletter promotion

The members are seeking to establish whether Lutnick blocked efforts to stop the suspected smuggling of advanced Nvidia chips to China while Cantor Fitzgerald held hundreds of millions of dollars in Nvidia shares. The firm says those holdings largely reflected positions used to hedge client trades and denies wrongdoing.

The buildup of pressure suggests that Lutnick could become the first major test of Congress’s efforts to bring the Trump administration to book.

Bardella, a former spokesperson for the House oversight committee, observed: “Democratic lawmakers, when they take power in January, are going to want to air this out in public. They’re going to want to know who at commerce decided not to blacklist Megaspeed in spite of objections from four other agencies.

“Did Lutnick make the call himself? What did his deputy authorise when having conversations with Nvidia’s top lawyer? In my experience, the more information comes out, the less great it gets for the target of the oversight. Lutnick has a rough three to six months ahead.”

Some are already demanding his departure. Richard Blumenthal, a Democratic senator for Connecticut, tweeted this week : “Lutnick must go. His malign self-enriching malfeasance shows the costs of corruption – putting personal profit above public interest.”

Steve Schmidt , a former Republican campaign strategist, said in a phone interview: “He should be fired. He’s utterly disloyal to the country without question. There are facts that have been asserted in newspapers about the conflicts of interest and his profiteering on the sale of these chips, and the sale of these chips has undermined American security.”

Lutnick accompanied Trump on his trip to Asia last week. When the president returned to the White House on Friday, he assured reporters that he had not lost confidence in the commerce secretary. “He’s a different kind of a guy. A very good businessman … He’s a natural businessman … I think he’s doing a very good job.”

However, Trump has previously offered officials public assurances of support shortly before showing them the door. Schmidt commented: “Trump realises he’s a buffoon. Lutnick has abused his relationship with Trump in a way that Trump doesn’t particularly care for and he won’t be long for this world.”

Lutnick has survived political turbulence before. Earlier this year he weathered calls to resign after acknowledging that he had visited Jeffrey Epstein’s private Caribbean island with his family in 2012, despite previously saying he had cut off contact with the convicted sex offender in 2005.

Reed Galen , founder of Civic Forum and a former Republican strategist, said: “It would be great if Lutnick resigned but, given that no one in any position in this administration has any sense of morality or shame, why would he think he’s done anything wrong? If a fish rots from the head then Lutnick is only doing what he has been shown is completely acceptable behaviour.”

The commerce department did not respond to a request for comment.

stories.body:
MP Sir Andrew Mitchell has campaigned for publicly accessible registers of who owns companies in British Overseas Territories and Crown Dependencies

Published 22 November 2026, 07:22 GMT

Plans to improve transparency over company ownership in Guernsey and Jersey have come under criticism from a Westminster MP, who says they "do not go nearly far enough".

The comments come after Guernsey , external and Jersey , external set out plans to allow approved applicants access to information about who owns or controls companies when investigating suspected financial crime.

Sir Andrew Mitchell, who has campaigned for greater scrutiny of company ownership, said there were "immediate indications" the proposals would fall short.

He said limits on access to the information could mean "national security threats may remain entirely invisible to investigators".

The plans follow a joint commitment made by Guernsey, Jersey and the Isle of Man in December 2023 to increase transparency around company ownership and help tackle money laundering, terrorist financing and other financial crime.

Currently, information about who ultimately owns or controls companies is generally only available to law enforcement agencies, regulators and certain regulated businesses carrying out anti-money laundering checks.

The new proposals would allow journalists, academics and other applicants with a legitimate interest to apply for access.

'Defeats the object'

Sir Andrew said investigators could face a "catch-22" because they may need access to the register to prove wrongdoing in the first place.

He also said he understood applicants would have to show they had been unable to find the information elsewhere, arguing: "This entirely defeats the object of a register."

Jersey's consultation response says applicants would be expected to show that "all reasonable alternative sources have been exhausted" before access was granted.

Guernsey's published response does not explicitly set out the same requirement.

He said: "Access should be open to those from other jurisdictions, for example those in the global south from whom much of the world's dirty money was stolen in the first place."

Sir Andrew also questioned whether users would have to pay to access the information, saying: "This information should be free at the point of access."

He said the proposals should eventually lead to fully public registers.

'Effective transparency framework'

Both the governments of Guernsey and Jersey rejected Sir Andrew's criticism and said they continue to meet international standards in tackling financial crime.

A Government of Jersey spokesperson said the concerns raised by him "do not accurately reflect what is in Jersey's consultation response paper".

They said the policy was intended to help Jersey meet its international commitments while maintaining "a fair, proportionate, and effective transparency framework".

They added: "Jersey continues to meet international standards for transparency and countering money laundering, terrorist financing and proliferation financing."

'Tried and tested'

Deputy Andrew Niles, from Guernsey's Policy & Resources Committee, rejected Sir Andrew's criticism and pointed to a positive 2025 assessment of the island's efforts to tackle financial crime , external .

He said: "Guernsey does not accept the suggestion that our proposals fall short of the commitments we've made on beneficial ownership transparency or that the island does not meet international standards on beneficial ownership transparency."

He said the framework would provide access for people with a legitimate interest in investigating crime while protecting privacy and vulnerable individuals.

"The proposal is based on a tried and tested model adopted in the EU," he added.

stories.body:
Exclusive: Countries at Cop31 are being urged to commit to deriving 35% of their energy from electricity by 2035

China is pushing for rapid electrification of its economy using low-carbon energy and will help other countries do the same, a senior member of the Chinese delegation at the Cop31 UN climate summit has said.

Wang Yi, a professor of energy and environment policy at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and a senior adviser to China’s government, said: “End-use electrification is a very clear direction. We can follow this direction while making the source of electricity clean. That’s the way to go forward.”

China is the biggest emitter of greenhouse gases by far, producing more than a quarter of the world’s total, so its push for electrification is significant.

At Cop31, countries are being asked to sign up to a target of deriving 35% of final energy consumption from electricity by 2035 . Australia, the president of the negotiations, and the host nation Turkey have pushed the target and on Friday night Australia and China signed a joint statement endorsing the “35:35” goal.

But in the second draft text of the probable outcome from Cop31 , released on Thursday, the electrification pledge was downgraded to one of a suite of voluntary options countries can take up to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions.

In an interview with the Guardian at the talks, Wang said: “China will do our best to realise clean end-use electrification, and also help other countries to improve. China has significantly reduced the cost of clean technology and products and we would like to share our experience with other countries.”

Experts have said electrification is the next vital step in the shift to a low-carbon economy, as the only way to diminish the close to 80% of fossil fuels still used for primary energy, mostly for transport, heating and industry.

While civil society organisations want any commitment made on electrification to specify that it must be met from clean sources, a pledge that leaves the choice to countries is likely to have more widespread support, as many – including China and India – are resistant to anything they feel smacks of “top down” interference in national plans.

But campaigners argue that allowing individual countries to decide risks leaving the door open to more gas-fired power plants. Some compromise language is also possible that would urge countries to decarbonise their power.

Last year, electricity made up nearly 30% of China’s energy use and it is on track to make that 35% by 2030. Electricity is several times more efficient than fossil fuels , meaning that it takes far less energy to run electric vehicles, heat pumps and industrial processes than their fossil fuel counterparts.

Wang said China was happy with the 2035 target, but that it would be harder to meet if the electricity was required to come entirely from low-carbon sources. “For this target, no problem. But if you think about ensuring clean electrification, that may be a little bit difficult, even for China. For other countries, it’s even more difficult,” he said.

China still has a large number of coal-fired power stations and is planning some new ones, though fewer than before. Wang said this would be used for back-up during the transition to clean energy.

One of the key issues at Cop31 is the “transition away from fossil fuels”, which was one of the resolutions passed at the Cop28 summit in Dubai in 2023 , but which countries have failed to flesh out since. The phrase was included in the first draft of the “cover decision” outcome from Cop31, presented on Monday , but excised from the second draftissued on Thursday, to the dismay of many countries and campaigners .

after newsletter promotion

Wang said: “We agree with paragraph 28 of the UAE consensus [the transition resolution]. But maybe different countries have different roadmaps. It’s very difficult to have only one unified roadmap for every country. So maybe we will help other countries to have their own country-based solutions, to realise their own national way of establishing a new renewable-based power system.”

China is also concerned about trade barriers to its clean technology exports, including the tariffs that the US under Donald Trump has placed on Chinese goods, and the “carbon border adjustment mechanism” (CBAM) imposed by the EU. The CBAM penalises imports from countries with looser regulations on carbon than the EU , which forces companies in high-carbon sectors to pay for their carbon emissions in order to level the playing field.

Some smaller developing countries have criticised the EU for its CBAM, warning that it will hamper their manufacturing industries. The EU said it had processes in place to ensure smaller developing countries were not hurt.

Wang called for more work on trade issues at Cops. “They must come together to find a unified approach,” he said. “China and other developing countries, including the global south, disagree [with the EU] on this. But that’s why we should continue to strengthen our dialogue.”

Jiangwen Guo, a senior research fellow at the Chatham House thinktank, said other countries could learn from China. “China has very consistent top-down policies [and] sets a clear direction with high consistency, then follows with learning by doing,” she said. “In the great energy transition, there is no one ahead of China. China is creating the model for the globe.”

Negotiators at Cop31, which was scheduled to end at 6pm on Friday, were sent home late on Friday after the talks stalled , with a new draft text of a “cover decision” marking the main outcome of the negotiations not thought likely to emerge until some time on Saturday morning. The talks are likely to continue into Saturday and potentially beyond.

stories.title: Spitting Image co-creator Peter Fluck dies aged 85
stories.summary: The 85-year-old he died in the early hours of Saturday at home in Cornwall, following a recent illness.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Peter Fluck alongside a satirical puppet of Margaret Thatcher that he created, pictured in 1992

Published 21 November 2026

Peter Fluck, co-creator of award-winning satirical puppet show Spitting Image, has died aged 85.

His family said he died in the early hours of Saturday at home in Cornwall, following a recent illness.

Spitting Image was immensely popular and sometimes controversial, running from 1984-1996 across 18 seasons, and featured puppet caricatures of celebrities, politicians and royals, including former Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher and Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother.

"The spirit that Spitting Image brought to the country was epoch defining," a family statement said.

"With Roger Law ('Luck and Flaw'), he brought a unique cutting edge to caricaturing that later evolved into a production company that created the TV series Spitting Image," it added.

"Peter's creative life continued after the series for many years from his studio in Cornwall. He was a private man who eschewed fame and attention."

The show won several awards, including one Bafta TV award and two Emmys and at its peak drew an audience of 15 million.

Fluck was born in Cambridge in 1941, and created the show alongside childhood friend Roger Law, who he met while studying at Cambridge School of Art.

Following school, both Fluck and Law moved to London and set up as freelance illustrators, and in 1976 set up their partnership 'Luck and Flaw' back in Cambridge.

Peter Fluck (left) and Roger Law in 1984

"You could say we took the traditional newspaper editorial cartoon and put it on the screen," Fluck told ArtCornwall in an interview , external in 2006.

He described the show as being shown "at the difficult time of 10 o'clock on a Sunday night when all politicians should have been in bed".

Many of the characters included parodies of Thatcher's cabinet, with Douglas Hurd depicted with "Mr Whippy ice cream" hair, and her successor John Major caricatured as a dull, grey puppet with a penchant for peas.

"We did get quite a lot of approaches from politicians for their puppet to be made, because if you didn't appear as a puppet on Spitting Image you hadn't made it as a politician," Fluck said in an interview in 2011. , external

It was eventually axed by ITV because of declining audience numbers.

In a statement, the broadcaster said Fluck's "creative contribution to TV satire is simply unrivalled... his cutting edge puppetry and caricature skills, alongside the show's sharp and always shrewdly observed humour, became a defining part of the cultural zeitgeist.

"Our thoughts and deepest sympathies are with his family and friends at this very sad time."

When he stepped away from the show, Fluck moved to Cornwall and focused his art on ceramics, printmaking and mobiles.

In 2018, Law donated his entire archive of Spitting Images to Cambridge University.

The collection - including original scripts, puppet moulds, drawings and recordings - was conserved and held in the library.

stories.title: UK should only rejoin EU if it innovates on technology, Blair warns
stories.summary: The former prime minister argues the European Union is probably moving in the wrong direction on technology innovation.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Tony Blair, a prominent opponent of leaving the EU, has said "Brexit was a real mistake"

Published 21 November 2026

Former prime minister Sir Tony Blair has said Britain should only rejoin the European Union if it reforms - and allows more innovation on technology.

Speaking to The Sunday Times , external , Sir Tony said: "I was painted as saying Britain should just go back and rejoin - I'm not saying that - it's heavily conditioned."

Sir Tony was a prominent opponent of leaving the EU, and told the paper: "I do think Brexit was a real mistake."

But he added the debate was different now than it was in 2016.

Referencing the need for technology innovation, he said Europe could and "probably are" moving in the wrong direction.

He said: "The problem if we go back and join Europe is that; I can't say that the technology revolution is the single biggest thing, and then if Europe moves in the wrong direction on technology innovation, which they might do and presently probably are doing, that it's a good idea for Britain to rejoin. That's what's changed in this last ten years."

He argued Britain should have an ambition to reform the EU.

But he added that we have to be "prepared to walk away from that negotiation" and need to make our own economy and tech sector strong.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham this week agreed what he called a "win-win" deal with the EU.

The agreement covered British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen also announced that the trading bloc and the UK are launching a digital partnership, including areas like artificial intelligence (AI) and quantum technology.

The EU and Britain "have enormous potential to innovate together", she added.

PM Andy Burnham met EU chief Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa in Brussels on Friday

On artificial intelligence, Sir Tony said that "AI is like fire - it can cook your food and burn your house down".

Sir Tony said the risks of AI are "very considerable" and that tech "can be used for good or bad".

"It's a new world," he said.

He added other countries are "coming up and rising and there is a dynamism and energy in them" and he fears the UK is "not as dynamic and energetic as we need to be".

Burnham was in Brussels on Friday to finalise the latest stage of the government's post-Brexit "reset" of relations with the EU - which originally began under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.

European Council President António Costa said the EU remains "open to have the closest possible relationship" with the UK.

The prime minister added that beyond the deal "we do need to consider what is the right long-term relationship".

He said over the coming months before the next UK-EU summit both sides will "seek to conduct an informal brainstorming process" to look at what those options are.

He fell short of discussing whether the UK could rejoin the EU.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the UK-EU deal "isn't fair" - and Reform's Nigel Farage called it a "betrayal of the British people".

Earlier this year, Sir Tony urged PM Andy Burnham to restart negotiations on the possibility of the UK rejoining the EU - but with caveats.

Writing in a paper from the Tony Blair Institute for Global Change , external published in September, the former prime minister wrote: "We should be clear that we want back into a formal relationship with the EU. But it must be a Europe on a credible path to reform."

"This is not about rerunning the debates of 2016 but taking a new approach rooted in the reality of 2026," he added.

stories.body:
President gives wide-ranging White House press conference and says he has ‘fantastic relationships’ with Putin and Xi

Donald Trump threatened on Friday to impose “tremendous penalties” on American tech companies that build datacenters outside the US, though he gave no details and told reporters he had not yet informed his own officials about the plan.

In a discursive press conference from the White House briefing room, Trump also said he would “look into” the report that Iran had been planning to possibly detonate a “dirty bomb” in Washington DC, and backed JD Vance over comments the vice-president made blaming Republican midterm losses on the Iran war.

Trump also expounded on his friendship with the Russian president Vladimir Putin, whom he met alongside China’s Xi Jinping at the Apec summit on Thursday, adding he had “fantastic relationships” with both autocratic leaders.

At the White House, Trump told reporters he wanted datacenters built by US companies to stay on US soil.

“We’re not allowing datacenters to go into other countries, because China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen. And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try to do it,” he said.

He said Americans should welcome datacenters, and urged communities to extract concessions from developers, repeating a point he made before the midterms.

“You ought to take advantage of the datacenters. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but don’t shut them off,” he said.

“We want them to build it here.”

With many Americans turning against the datacenters being built near their homes, the US tech industry is making a show of conciliation by promising to take fewer government handouts, to be more transparent, and to give more money to towns and cities willing to allow server warehouses to be built.

The Trump administration on Monday issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced US computing chips and servers, in a move it said was designed to limit China’s ability to use US chips to train its artificial intelligence models – though a House committee said on Wednesday the US had signed off on sales of nearly 900,000 AI chips to China in six months.

China’s ability to obtain advanced AI chips made by the US firm Nvidia, in which Trump is an investor, has been spotlighted in recent weeks after its CEO, Jensen Huang, was fired over his affair with a woman alleged to be spying for China.

In the same press conference, Trump was asked about reports Iran was planning to potentially detonate an explosive laced with nuclear material – a so-called “dirty bomb” – in Washington DC. The president called it a “rumour” and said: “If they do, we’re going to fight.”

He added: “We know a lot about what’s happening in Iran. We know everything they say. We know who they are, where they are. We’ll find out about it.”

Responding to a question about reports of a rift with Vance, Trump said the vice-president’s remark blaming the Republican collapse on the Iran war was “a very accurate statement”.

“I didn’t say I was unhappy with it,” the president said. “I would have added one other thing if it were asked … would you do it again? And absolutely, the answer is yes, because we cannot allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.”

Trump was asked whether Vladimir Putin could really be considered a friend to America since Russia is a close ally of Iran.

“I can’t speak to America,” he said, adding: “I consider [that] I have fantastic relationships with Putin. That’s a very good thing. I have fantastic relationships with President Xi. That’s a good thing, and our country is safe because of that.”

He praised Putin as he repeated his grievances over the Department of Justice’s investigation into the Russian attempts to influence US voters ahead of the 2016 presidential election.

“I’ve been dealing with Putin … [since] the fake Russia, Russia, Russia hoax,” he said.

Trump also spoke about two prominent Democrats. He said Gina Hinojosa, who won the race for Texas governor over Trump’s Republican ally Greg Abbott, called him. “She was really nice,” Trump said. “It was a very productive call. And she wants to have a strong border, and I think we’ll be able to work something out.”

And he said Hakeem Jeffries – who Trump previously called a “thug” but is now in line to be the next speaker of the House, and the first Black speaker – is “a smart guy. He’s a streetwise guy.”

stories.title: First minister 'gobsmacked' by Burnham's devolution calls rejection
stories.summary: The prime minister says he is "not persuaded" by the argument that devolution would benefit Wales.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Rhun ap Iorwerth says the decision shows Westminster is disregarding the views of the people of Wales

Published 20 November 2026

Wales' First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth has declared he is "gobsmacked" after calls for powers to be handed from Westminster to Cardiff were snubbed.

In a letter to ap Iorwerth, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he was "not persuaded" by the case to devolve responsibilities over policing and justice, the Crown Estate and rail infrastructure to Wales.

The first minister told BBC Radio Wales Breakfast that "this is about Westminster saying, we decide, it doesn't matter what the people of Wales think".

Welsh Secretary Stephen Kinnock said the changes would have led to "destabilisation and fragmentation and disintegration".

The first minister said what Kinnock said was there had been a lot of engagement across the departments of the UK government in Whitehall, and not with Wales, and they "then decided that they didn't want Wales to be empowered on policing injustice in the Crown Estates and on rail".

He added: "I'm pretty gobsmacked by that, but at least one positive here is that we are seeing very clearly now that this is about Westminster saying, 'we decide, it doesn't matter what the people of Wales think'.

"We heard the secretary of state there saying that there's a variety of views on devolution.

"Yes, those views in Wales on one side and those in Westminster and Whitehall on the other."

Kinnock said there was "a bold and ambitious offer on the table there to work with the first minister on a whole range of issues around devolving fiscal powers, employment support, reindustrialisation, innovation and regional empowerment".

This was "to get power and growth closer to regional areas of Wales and local areas and communities", he said.

Former First Minister Mark Drakeford, said he was "disappointed" by Burnham's decision.

He said: "I don't think he quite understands how different things are when you talk about a country, with the Senedd.

"We'll just have to keep going within the Labour party internally to make the cause, to persuade people."

Ap Iorwerth earlier accused Burnham of "turning his back on devolution" and not viewing Wales as an "equal nation" after he decided against devolving the powers.

Burnham's position is also at odds with Welsh Labour leader Ken Skates who reiterated his position at a party conference last weekend that policing and the Crown Estate should be devolved.

Andy Burnham said he wanted to see "one Labour team" at the Welsh Labour Conference

The letter, seen by BBC Wales, follows what had been seen as positive talks between the prime minister and first minister in Glasgow last month.

Asked about the prime minister's position on devolving policing following that meeting, ap Iorwerth said: "I think instinctively the prime minister wants to go there."

Burnham had also previously said he was "open" to the idea.

However, in his letter on Friday, Burnham said he was "not persuaded" by the case.

"The integrated England and Wales policing system is essential to maintaining interoperability, enabling seamless cross-border working and ensuring forces in Wales can draw on national and specialist capabilities," Burnham said.

"Retaining that integrated framework helps ensure policing in Wales can respond effectively to threats and to protecting the public," he added.

On justice, Burnham said he "strongly believes" the current devolution settlement enables Wales to "benefit from the resources, expertise and resilience" of a shared justice system.

"Effective partnership working is therefore essential to improving outcomes for victims, reducing reoffending and building safer communities."

The Crown Estate includes the seabed off the Welsh coast.

The land belongs to the reigning monarch, and the revenue from its property portfolio goes directly to the UK Treasury.

The level of profit generated from the Crown Estate is used as a benchmark to calculate the funding given by the government to the Royal Family

The previous Welsh Labour government as well as the current Plaid Cymru administration have long called for it to be devolved.

The prime minister told members of his party last week that Welsh Labour may have lost sight of some of the principles of devolution before it was thrown out of power in a historic election defeat .

However, in his letter Burnham said the Crown Estate's "current model provides the best means of maximising the economic and social benefits for Wales".

He went on to say the UK government was "not persuaded by the case for devolving the management of the Crown Estate in Wales, nor to prepare for a future transfer".

Finally, on rail infrastructure, Burnham told the first minister: "I believe funding and delivery of infrastructure is best done by the new Great British Railways, in collaboration with Transport for Wales and Welsh government.

"I am therefore not persuaded by the case for full devolution of rail infrastructure, as it would fragment the current system and affect the service provided to the public by the highly integrated cross border network."

A spokesperson for the first minister accused the prime minister of "turning his back on devolution".

"His warm words on devolution are now ringing hollow and there is no longer any doubt that when he talks of driving power out of Whitehall, he only means to the regions of England," they said.

The spokesperson added that Burnham's "refusal to even explore the devolution of the Crown Estate, justice and policing, and rail infrastructure proves that the prime minister does not view Wales as an equal nation."

stories.title: Scouts say they face £1m tourist tax cost for overnight trips
stories.summary: The increased cost after the proposed Visitors Levy is imposed could price some young people out of joining Scout camps and other trips, the group said.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 21 November 2026

Scout groups are warning they could face an additional annual bill of £1m as a result of the government's proposed tourist tax for England.

The overnight levy would allow councils and regional authorities to charge visitors an additional fee for their accommodation, including campsites, raising money to be spent on local services.

The increased cost from the Visitors Levy could price some young people out of joining Scout camps and other trips, the group said.

Dwayne Fields, the UK's Chief Scout, has called for youth groups to be exempted and said the charity - which sees more than 1.4m overnight stays a year - would be "firmly opposed to any proposal that would see local mayors tax Scouts and other voluntary youth organisations".

The Ministry of Housing, Communities & Local Government told the BBC that local leaders who introduce the levy "will have the option to exempt certain types of accommodation in their areas, including accommodation which is often used for trips by youth groups like Scouts and Girl Guides - such as camping pitches".

They added money raised from the levy will "stay local and be invested in the visitor experience and local growth including in high streets, parks and events".

Labour mayors have indicated they would cap the levy at 5% but the legislation contains no maximum limit.

In a statement, the Scout Association said the tax, if set at 5% across the country, could cost the charity £1.04m a year and force volunteers to deal with onerous paperwork.

They worked this out by assuming the levy would be set at 5% for all the 1,423,344 annual overnight stays across Squirrels, Beavers, Cubs, Scouts, Explorers and volunteers.

Girlguiding would also be subject to the levy.

In a statement, Fields said: "We strongly support investment being made available to strengthen local communities. Well-crafted legislation can unlock that opportunity.

"But we are firmly opposed to any proposal that would see local mayors tax Scouts and other voluntary youth organisations for camping trips that equip young people with skills for life, while burdening volunteers with the role of unpaid government tax collectors."

Manchester Scout volunteer Chris Taylor called the proposals "madness"

Chris Taylor, lead volunteer for Greater Manchester East Scout County, called the levy a "tent tax" and branded it "madness".

Referring to the levy being applied to the Linnet Clough campsite run by his group in Stockport, he said: "Our members spent nearly 25,000 nights away from home last year, and a 5% levy would add over £11,000 a year to the cost of their camps and sleepovers."

He added: "On top of that, and as a charity, we'd have to employ someone just to collect the tax and send returns to the Mayor's office. That's another £7,000 a year, and that's just one campsite - there are plenty more across Manchester."

Labour MP Gareth Snell, who challenged ministers when the levy was debated in the House of Commons , said Scouts "provide some of the most memorable experiences for young people up and down the country."

The Stoke-on-Trent Central MP called on the government to take the decision out of mayors' hands and ensure Scout camps are exempted from the bill.

The Welsh Government has announced young people staying in hostels, campsites or outdoor centres would be exempt from its tourism tax, due to come into effect next year.

stories.title: Deal with EU not dependent on tuition fees agreement, Miliband says
stories.summary: Brussels sources had previously suggested the bloc might not apply the wider deal until fees were lowered for EU students in Britain.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

This video can not be played

Watch: Miliband spoke to the BBC following the summit in Brussels

Published 21 November 2026

A deal agreed between the UK and the European Union on Friday will come into force regardless of whether the two sides can negotiate a separate tuition fees agreement, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has told the BBC.

The measures agreed in Brussels include scrapping most checks on British food exports in return for the UK following some EU regulations from 2028, and a new youth mobility scheme.

However, a proposal from the bloc to lower the level of tuition fees paid by EU students in the UK has not been agreed.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she was "confident" a solution would be found, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham adding "me too" during a press conference announcing the deal.

Meanwhile, asked in his interview with the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme whether rejoining the EU would be looked at, Miliband said "all the options will be on the table".

It came after the prime minister said that he would discuss possible ideas for even closer ties with the bloc in the coming months.

What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start? Published 2 days ago

Burnham gets his first taste of EU dealmaking and seems hungry for more Published 2 days ago

Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow Published 2 days ago

UK and EU leaders have hailed the closer cooperation agreement, with Burnham calling the deal a "win-win" that could lower the cost of living and reduce red tape.

The prime minister said the Treasury believes the deal could boost the UK economy by up to £17bn a year.

EU sources had earlier suggested that the bloc might hold up applying the wider deal until it was agreed that EU students who wanted to study in the UK would pay the same fees as British students.

Miliband said it was "absolutely clear" the agreements on food exports, energy and youth mobility would apply, even though there has not been a deal on tuition fees.

"President von der Leyen... was very clear about this at the press conference we just had. She said there are those three agreements and then there's a separate piece of paper and a separate issue, which is looking at the issue of tuition," he said.

Asked again whether the agreements would definitely become law, the foreign secretary said: "Yes, absolutely."

"The dates are set out in 2028 when these things are coming in, we're introducing legislation in Parliament, so definitely."

Miliband said there would be "no cost" to the UK taxpayer for anything agreed at Friday's summit, adding that there would be no new contributions to the EU budget.

He said previously announced agreements on EU schemes like Erasmus+ were a "separate decision" and the summit "was not about cost to the taxpayer".

Speaking on Friday, Burnham argued that polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".

Miliband told the BBC that "of course all the options will be on the table" when pressed on whether rejoining the bloc would be considered, adding that "we will look at the benefits and the costs of all the different options".

He said that while he accepted the result of the 2016 Brexit referendum, "the world has changed massively".

"Europe is changing too, so we've got to look at what that means. It's not about this parliament, we're respecting the red lines in this parliament," he added.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal was "not fair", arguing that UK farmers would have to follow rules set in Brussels and young people from the EU would "compete" with young Britons struggling to get jobs at home.

She also claimed Burnham had "plucked" the £17bn figure out of thin air, and said the only modelling she had seen of how the agreement could boost the economy put the figure at "0.0%".

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said Friday marked a "betrayal of the British people" and a good day for the EU to "try and humiliate" the UK.

Farage, who was a leading figure in the 2016 campaign to get Britain out of the EU, wrote on social media: "Like every prime minister before him, Burnham is a total fraud."

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said there needed to be more than "tweaks" to the UK's relationship to the EU.

"A youth mobility scheme is a big step forward, but it's nowhere near enough. We need a whole new deal that actually works for Britain, and fast."

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, the University of Manchester's vice chancellor Professor Duncan Ivison said closer UK-EU relations were a "good thing" but "the issue of tuition fees is something we do have to figure out because there is a cost".

He warned that EU students being allowed to pay domestic university fees would "take £500m, we estimate, out of the higher education sector at a time where there's a lot of pressure on the sector".

He added: "If EU students come and are paying domestic fees, it's not clear we'd be able to increase the number of places for EU students anyway."

Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle said the Treasury and Department for Education would work with universities to find a solution during negotiations.

She told BBC Breakfast: "I don't think anybody wants to do deals that negatively impact anything. We want win-win deals."

stories.body:
Surge fuelled by ‘preppers’ heeding Be Ready campaign’s call for households to have three days of food and water for emergencies

Retail sales in Great Britain surged last month as the public rushed to buy products including tinned food and long-life milk, after the government issued a warning to stock up in case of a disaster.

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said the volume of goods sold jumped by 0.7% month on month in October, defying economists’ consensus expectations of flat sales, as “preppers” took heed of the government’s Be Ready campaign to hold supplies to last 72 hours to survive a possible extreme weather event, cyber incident or another serious emergency.

The surge in sales is a welcome bounce back for the industry after a poor September , which the ONS has revised down from a 0.4% fall to a 0.6% fall, fuelled in part by poor online sales of autumn and winter clothing because of unseasonably warm weather.

“Supermarkets have told us that sales of long-life food items such as tinned food and UHT milk were boosted by the government’s Be Ready campaign,” said Grant Fitzner, the chief economist at the ONS.

Food store sales, primarily supermarkets, rose by 0.8% month on month, the fastest rate since the 1.4% rise in April.

Oliver Vernon-Harcourt, the head of retail at Deloitte, said: “Consumers responded to the government’s Be Ready campaign by stocking up on long-life grocery items, which reflects a broader attitude from shoppers to prioritise essentials.”

But Paul Dales, the chief UK economist at Capital Economics , said the jump in household “prepping” could mean slower food sales growth in the coming months.

“The cupboards only need to be stocked once for this, hopefully,” he told clients. “It seems unlikely that households can continue to spend at this rate with a further energy-induced rise in inflation around the corner.”

Separate data last week showed that British shoppers had been stocking up on essentials such as bottled water, tinned goods and hand sanitiser in preparation for possible emergencies.

The ONS also reported that textile, clothing and footwear stores reported a 1.5% month-on-month boost in October. An increase in visits to galleries, and a jump in sales of sports equipment, games and toys, lifted sales across other non-food stores by 3.1% month-on-month, the biggest rise since January.

The total non-food stores category – which includes department stores, clothing, household and other non-food stores – increased by 1.1% month on month in October.

after newsletter promotion

Non-store retail sales, primarily online but also sellers such as street stalls and markets, bounced back too, rising 0.9% as a turn in the weather last month drove sales of autumn and winter ranges.

However, sales volumes of motor fuel fell by 2.2% last month, the steepest rate since April, as prices at the pump rose.

“October’s retail sales have exceeded expectations, despite low consumer confidence and growing pressure on household finances from higher interest rates and inflation,” said Erin Brookes, the European retail and consumer lead at Alvarez & Marsal.

“Retailers will be feeling optimistic as the sector approaches the critical Black Friday and Christmas trading period, with October’s sales growth suggesting consumers are still willing to spend this festive season.

“Despite this positivity, retailers are caught between increasingly price-sensitive consumers and mounting operating costs.”

stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The US president rated his summit with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin as 12 out of 10 but China and Russia had the most to celebrate

H e got by with a little help from his friends. Rebuked by millions of voters in a still resilient democracy, Donald Trump travelled to Asia this week and found comfort in the company of autocrats who still flatter him.

The US president, reduced to lame-duck status at home by a humiliating midterm election defeat, returned to the global stage in a meeting with two strongmen in Shenzhen, China, that critics described as a new low for America’s claim to moral authority.

“ Who is he? ” Trump asked rhetorically, pointing as he walked towards the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin. “He’s my friend.” Separately he told the Chinese president, Xi Jinping: “You’re my friend, and we have a very special relationship.”

Trump, Xi and Putin convened at the Kylin Villa in Shenzhen, China, for the first-ever trilateral summit among the leaders of the US, China and Russia, the world’s three biggest nuclear powers. The official product of their 70-minute closed-door meeting was a four-point document titled the “Declaration Toward Peace” that made no mention of the wars in Iran or Ukraine.

But the defining image was of the trio sitting around a huge circular wooden table. At its hollow centre sat an immaculate arrangement of pink flowers, an ancient Chinese motif meant to evoke harmony. To US-based critics, however, the optics sent a different signal.

Steve Schmidt , a former adviser to George W Bush and John McCain, said: “The image of the grotesque large round table with a war criminal dictator, a stable dictator and an irrational, delusional wannabe dictator is an image of deep shame and weakness for the United States.

“It’s a repudiation of American values, American honour, common sense and the national security interests of the country, and a betrayal of America’s allies all across the world.”

Beijing understood how to satisfy the Trump ego. When Air Force One landed in Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit, Xi made the unusual move of greeting Trump personally on the tarmac. An honour guard stood at attention, crowds waved miniature US and Chinese flags, schoolchildren shook pompoms and Xi drew Trump into a warm embrace.

Trump took the bait with delight. For him, victory was not measured in negotiating concessions but in the lavish banquet and the seat reserved for him at the head table. “That’s a big win for us,” he said in a TV interview. “It’s a big win for China too. We get along.” Trump was even treated to a performance of YMCA, the signature song of his campaign rallies.

In their first meeting since failed negotiations in Alaska last year, Trump held one-on-one talks with Putin that touched on Ukraine but secured no immediate commitments. The meeting occurred against a backdrop of Trump recently rejecting new sanctions on Russia.

In a bilateral meeting with Xi, Trump raised the US-led war in Iran, emphasising a joint interest in fully reopening the strait of Hormuz and preventing Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons. Xi focused on US-China trade stability and asserted China’s sovereign position on Taiwan, treating it as an unalterable domestic issue.

In one ominous remark, Trump told Xi: “I think as long as you and I are in charge of things, we’ll never have a problem.” He later told NBC News that the pair had also agreed that artificial intelligence needed some form of safety “guardrails” but offered few details.

The main event was the trilateral summit, with observers watching body language closely for any clues about the dynamics among Xi, relishing his role as host, Putin, whose war in Ukraine is faltering, and Trump, ostensibly the most powerful of the three but politically wounded at home. To many, it offered little more than a glorified photo op.

Brett Bruen , the president of the public affairs agency Global Situation Room and the former global engagement director of the Barack Obama White House, said: “Brand Trump has been badly sullied by a historic defeat at the hands of American voters. However, this isn’t going to improve his standing internationally and certainly not domestically.

“If anything, it put on display his desperation. It put on display his isolation internationally from the very people that he’s going to need to be able to secure trade deals or peace deals. Once again he’s returning from China with the luggage hold empty of any diplomatic accomplishments.”

The formal output of the summit was a study in profound omissions and authoritarian wishlists. The text made no mention of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, nor of the spiralling US military conflict with Iran.

Instead, the trio agreed on four broad points: pledging dialogue to reduce nuclear risks, committing to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum, calling for “reforms” to the United Nations and declaring that state sovereignty and the immunity of state officials must be respected while warning that the international criminal court (ICC) must not abuse its jurisdiction.

Putin currently faces an active ICC arrest warrant for war crimes in Ukraine, while the Trump administration has sanctioned ICC officials to shield itself and its ally Israel from judicial scrutiny.

Ned Price , a former deputy to the US representative to the UN, said: “The joint statement was notable, not because Russia and China said it, but because the United States also co-signed.

“The United Nations they want is not a United Nations that’s more effective but rather a United Nations that is less effective at upholding the rules of the road, the very principles that have been at the centre of the UN system since its founding: the idea that big countries can’t bully small countries, that borders can’t be redrawn by force.”

The talks have done little to dispel the impression that Trump regards Congress, the media and elections as pesky encumbrances while gazing with awe and some envy at Xi and Putin. As the Shenzhen summit concluded, European leaders and Nato officials convened urgently in Berlin to reinforce their support for Ukraine and resist any high-level partitioning of European security.

The summit was a propaganda win for Putin, who went from international pariah status to equal billing with the world’s two biggest economies. It was also a victory for Xi. Without making any concessions on Taiwan, trade tariffs or its industrial lifeline to Moscow, China positioned itself as the arbiter of 21st-century diplomacy.

“Xi was able to burnish China’s diplomatic sway and give Putin and Trump something that each leader respectively coveted,” said Ali Wyne , senior research and advocacy adviser for US-China relations at the International Crisis Group. “He gave Putin the opportunity to demonstrate that despite Russia’s wartime losses, despite western sanctions, Russia remains a great power.

“He gave Trump the opportunity to demonstrate, at least in Trump’s own mind, that despite these bruising midterm elections, Trump is a singularly visionary and consequential peacemaker, thereby appealing to Trump’s ego.”

While neither Beijing nor Moscow harbours any illusions about Trump’s volatile temperament, both recognise the ticking clock on his second term and know they are likely to outlast him.

Wyne added: “Both of them recognise that it is next to impossible that any of President Trump’s successors will view them in comparable terms as friends, adopt conciliatory dispositions, and on certain issues come close to aligning US positions with those of China and Russia.”

Although he was caught on camera apparently nodding off, Trump departed China appearing politically rejuvenated after his encounters with his two “friends”. He hailed the visit as “Highly Consequential” on social media and said later: “On a scale of zero to 10, I think it was a 12.”

Staff gagging clauses lifted ahead of probe into culture at data watchdog
stories.summary: Ministers are expected to publish the details of how an independent review of the working environment at the Information Commission will be carried out next week.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 21 November 2026

Non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) signed by staff at the UK's information watchdog will be lifted to allow them to speak out about its culture, the government has confirmed.

Ministers are expected to publish the details of how an independent review of the working environment at the Information Commission will be carried out next week.

It follows the departure of the watchdog's boss five months ago amid allegations of sexually inappropriate behaviour.

A government spokesperson confirmed that NDAs, known as "gagging clauses", would not be enforced by the Information Commission, saying the regulator "will not use the terms of any agreement to prevent people from participating in the review".

The government "will set out further details on the review, including its terms of reference and the independent reviewer, shortly", they added.

The Information Commission is one of the UK's most high-profile regulators charged with the crucial task of regulating AI, data protection and Freedom of Information requests.

It recently won a court battle with TikTok after it fined the social media platform £12.7m for misusing children's data, and has penalised bodies including the Ministry of Defence after an email blunder exposed the details of interpreters fleeing Afghanistan.

But it has been without permanent leadership since Information Commissioner John Edwards resigned earlier this year .

It came after an independent investigation found a "case to answer" over reports of alleged inappropriate behaviour towards staff including claims of sexual harassment.

The Information Commission said the investigation found Edwards' behaviour "fell short of the conduct expected from a public official".

In a resignation statement posted on his LinkedIn page in June, Edwards said he disagreed with how the investigation had been carried out but accepted his position had "become untenable".

The statement continued: "I have accepted that there have been occasions where I exercised poor judgement and made attempts at humour that were inappropriate and caused offence."

Freedom of Information requests have found that since the start of Edwards' tenure in 2022 to the present, 16 current and former employees have signed non-disclosure or confidentiality clauses costing more than £354,000.

Nine of those , external included a "non-derogatory clause" which legally prevents employees from making negative comments publicly.

While this is a small proportion of the more than 1,000 staff employed by the commissioner, government advice stipulates that public bodies should only use confidentiality clauses "when necessary" and that they should "not seek to stifle or discourage staff from raising concerns".

Since 2025, new laws also mean they cannot be used to silence employees subjected to harassment or abuse.

After Edwards' departure, the government announced a review , external into the Commission's culture and governance, with the then-Secretary of State for Science, Innovation and Technology Liz Kendall telling a committee of MPs she was "absolutely appalled at what the independent investigator found - sexual harassment and bullying".

Five months later, the investigation has not begun.

In recent weeks, the two major civil service unions, the PCS and FDA, have pushed for an external examination of the events leading up to Edwards' resignation in meetings with government officials.

The unions have also asked for those who signed non-disclosure agreements with the ICO to be released from them so they can contribute to the review.

The PCS union says other concerns had previously been raised with them about Edwards, including a bullying complaint, which was investigated at the time.

An internal staff survey, published in August and released under FOI , external points towards wider issues at the Commission, with 14% of all employees reporting they had either personally experienced bullying, harassment and discrimination.

Multiple current and former employees have also told the BBC of experiencing or witnessing incidents of bullying or harassment.

PCS General Secretary Fran Heathcote said the union's members at the Commission "have been failed for too long by a toxic leadership culture that has allowed bullying and harassment to persist, leaving many staff fearful of speaking out".

Heathcote said she welcomed the "positive engagement" the union had received in recent weeks from the Commission and officials at the Department for Culture Media and Sport (DCMS), which oversees it.

But she added: "For the review to command the confidence of staff, it must be genuinely independent, robust in its approach, and prepared to identify where accountability lies."

Conservative MP Caroline Dinenage, who chairs the DCMS select committee, said the Commission "needed a firm new direction" after the departure of its former boss.

"Instead, a leadership vacuum has compounded what went before at a rudderless organisation where it seems the worst behaviours in the workplace are not being challenged," she added.

She said it was "vital" the government brought in "someone who can set a new tone and is dedicated to changing attitudes and protecting staff" to head up the Commission.

A spokesperson for the Information Commission said its commitment to an independent review reflected its "ongoing commitment to listening and learning from the events of the past year and those leading up to it".

"Our new Board, appointed this summer, has been working exceptionally hard to provide fresh leadership, ushering in a new governance structure and a new strategy," they added.

"It is committed to listening carefully to the review's findings and recommendations, and building on the positive work on our culture already taking place across the organisation."

stories.body:
Two weeks after Democrats flipped Congress, conservative outlets are having conversations on whether to distance themselves from Trump or double down on Maga

As a so-called “blue wave” crashed across the country on the night of 3 November, conservative hosts and commentators on Fox News displayed an almost virtuosic ability to avoid directly blaming Donald Trump for the Republican party’s defeat, instead pinning the blame on impertinent voters who didn’t grasp the strength of the economy.

“In some sense, Mr Trump was too successful in the first year and didn’t sell it enough in the second year,” said Larry Kudlow, a Fox Business Network host who served as the president’s director of the National Economic Council during his first administration.

But two weeks on, Trump’s electoral wipeout is facilitating difficult conversations about the future of the conservative media ecosystem – and whether outlets that target a Republican-voting audience need to create some distance from an unpopular president. Some other outlets, like the Maga-aligned Real America’s Voice News network, are planning to go the other direction and double down on Trump.

“The whole landscape can now be reordered, and I think it will be,” said Steve Bannon, a former chief strategist to Trump during his first administration who now hosts a show for Real America’s Voice.

Several conservative media personalities pinned the blame on Fox News for leading the party – and Trump – astray, with former host Tucker Carlson saying that the results signaled the end of “the Fox News era”. (Carlson didn’t respond to a message seeking comment.)

Bannon, who contends that Rupert Murdoch has long “hated Trump”, predicted that the network will utilize the party’s recent “rejection” at the polls to move away from Trump and embrace more traditional, George W Bush-era Republican priorities.

“They’re going to try to kick Trump into the dustbin,” he said. “They clearly have moved beyond Trump and they want to move beyond Trumpism … What they’re going to do is, with a thousand cuts, convince their ageing audience that Maga and what Maga stands for is too extreme.”

In contrast, Bannon said he expects Real America’s Voice and other outlets to “triple down” on the Maga movement and “populist nationalism.”

Bannon is not alone in his criticism of Murdoch’s media empire. Conservative commentator Ann Coulter said that she views the channel and its sister outlet, the New York Post, as “90% responsible for the GOP wipeout in the midterm elections”, blaming voices in the Murdoch media empire for encouraging Trump to launch – and sustain – an unpopular war against Iran.

Atlanta-based conservative radio host Erick Erickson said a realignment away from Trump will probably start in his medium before it carries over to conservative television – though he said it will take time, and will depend on how important access is for certain personalities.

“The more often you spend time at Mar-a-Lago, the less likely you are to distance yourself from Trump, because you still want in,” said Erickson, who vocally opposed Trump in 2016 before coming around ahead of his 2020 re-election bid.

Charlie Sykes, a former conservative radio host who also opposed Trump from the beginning, said the election has shown “cracks in that alternative reality silo” on Trump-aligned channels and platforms.

“In general, I think the scope of the blowout was just so great that even deep in the rightwing media ecosystem, they had to feel the tremors of it,” said Sykes, a former MS Now commentator who now writes on Substack . “And so that has been kind of interesting, this sense of like, ‘OK, we need to really come to grips with this and maybe figure out a way to move on.’”

Trump’s decision to attack Iran in February fomented division within the conservative media ecosystem, with many commentators viewing it as an abdication of his promise to abstain from foreign wars and focus on the US.

“I think those divisions are just going to widen,” Sykes said.

The Daily Caller, which was co-founded by Carlson in 2010 as something of a conservative alternative to the New York Times, made waves ahead of the midterms for calling out Trump’s war against Iran – and the high prices that have come out of it. “The Daily Caller is clearly positioning itself for a landscape not just post-midterms but post-Trump, and for a bitter and intensifying intraparty media battle,” the digital publication Semafor wrote on 1 November.

In an interview, Daily Caller editor-in-chief Amber Duke said the publication is more focused on reflecting the mood of the American people – particularly younger people affected by a challenging economy – than boosting Trump and the Maga movement.

“I think what we are doing is so unique that we are really setting ourselves apart,” she said. “We view ourselves as a principled, America-first outlet. I think there’s a difference between Maga and America-first.”

Duke also acknowledged the economic opportunities that drive support for the president. “Trump is a content goldmine. He drives a lot of traffic, a lot of clicks,” she said. “That content mine is eventually going to dry up. I would definitely be concerned if I had my entire business model tied around this uniquely celebrity-oriented newsmaker. How am I going to continue to stay in business after that? For us, it’s: Let’s just tell the truth to the American people, and that truth is not going to be dependent on any one person or political party.”

Some conservative outlets that are closely tied to Trump, however, don’t see any reason to do anything differently.

“Nothing changes with us,” Newsmax chief executive Christopher Ruddy said. “We’re going to continue reporting on the administration and we will continue to cover the Congress. We make a very concerted effort to always get both sides on our reports and in our TV opinion segments.”

Charles Herring, president of the far-right One America News Network, echoed that sentiment: “Our reporting doesn’t change based on the political pendulum or who resides in the White House. We are working hard every day to further enhance our coverage for our viewers.”

Still, there are limits to how far some conservative media organizations can stray from the president, considering the economic imperative to retain a pro-Trump audience. “The thing to understand about conservative media is that it’s not necessarily always top down,” Sykes said. “It’s often: What will the audience tolerate? … Nobody wants to get too crosswise with their audience.”

But the vast majority of conservative news sites have already seen declines in online traffic in recent months , according to industry tracker Howard Polskin, an early warning sign for the party’s midterm chances. “Audiences are not buying what Maga media is selling anymore,” he said.

“My prediction would be that in the next two years, rightwing media will become fractured with more infighting, breaking into two camps: pro-Maga/Trump and anti-Maga/Trump,” Polskin added. “Traffic to rightwing websites will continue to nose dive, much more so than mainstream media.”

Several conservative media veterans who spoke with the Guardian said the selection of a 2028 Republican presidential nominee will probably be a defining moment for the sector, and one that could split conservative media into different camps.

On the notion that vice-president JD Vance will be Trump’s heir apparent, Erickson said: “I actually am kind of encouraged by the level of pushback after the election that maybe this isn’t a good idea.” Brian Kilmeade, the co-host of the influential Fox News morning show Fox & Friends, has been particularly critical of Vance for seeming to distance himself from Trump’s decision-making on Iran. On his radio show this past week , Kilmeade said that Vance “never should have been vice-president” and that he’s “amazed that President Trump puts up with it”.

Over the next two years, conservative media personalities will have to put their chips down on a candidate. The challenge, Sykes said, is “figuring out where the audience is going, and getting there first”. He also expects conservative media outlets to prioritize attacking Democrats and undermining their control of Congress.

“It’s no longer about defense of Trump,” he added. “It’s like: What’s next? And everybody’s got to make that pivot.”

stories.body:
UK economy defies City predictions and Iran war fallout, with gap between spending and income about £1bn lower than expected in October, at £17bn

The UK government borrowed less than expected in October despite a rise in debt interest costs, in a boost for chancellor John Healey amid the pressure on Britain’s economy from the Middle East war.

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said public sector net borrowing – the difference between government spending and income – was £17bn in October, about £800m higher than the same month a year ago. City economists had forecast borrowing would increase by more, to £18bn.

In the financial year so far, public sector net borrowing was £111.3bn, the ONS said – £7.3bn less than in the same period last year, helped by stronger tax receipts.

The Office for Budget Responsibility, the independent Treasury watchdog, said the latest figures were “broadly in line” with its October forecast for a £1.1bn fall in total borrowing for the 2026-27 financial year. However, it warned there were “several risks” amid the sharp rise in energy costs, and public spending on cost of living support measures.

Grant Fitzner, the ONS chief economist, said: “Borrowing so far this financial year remained lower than in the same period last year with receipts growing faster than spending. Income-related taxes’ receipts grew particularly strongly.

“However, monthly borrowing was up on last October, partly down to higher debt interest.”

The latest figures showed rising borrowing costs on financial markets drove the UK’s debt interest payments to £11.2bn in October – £2.8bn more than in the same month last year, and the highest figure for any October since monthly records began in 1997.

Some government bonds are directly linked to the retail prices index measure of inflation, with payments rising in line with it. RPI has increased in recent months as the Iran war has pushed up energy costs.

Public sector net debt rose to £3.1tn, equivalent to 95.8% of GDP – 1.9 percentage points higher than last year and at levels last seen in the early 1960s.

Chief secretary to the Treasury, Emma Reynolds, said Britain was showing “standout resilience despite the global impact of the conflict in Iran.

“This year we’ve cut borrowing faster than any other G20 country. Now we’re going to cut waste and bureaucracy by reprioritising spending and making public services more efficient with AI,” Reynolds added.

Britain’s economy has continued to grow at the second-fastest rate in the G7 despite the fallout from the war in the Middle East, bolstered by AI investment and households continuing to spend.

In his budget last month, Healey raised taxes on banks to fund relief for households being squeezed by the energy shock from the Middle East war.

after newsletter promotion

Against a highly uncertain global backdrop, Healey stuck to the government’s fiscal rules with £15bn of headroom – less than the £23.6bn buffer left by his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, as the conflict drove up the UK government’s borrowing costs.

After a low-key budget statement designed with febrile bond markets in mind, economists warned the chancellor had set himself up for a “brutal” spending review next year.

Avoiding a return to austerity for unprotected government departments could require a £17bn top-up to the spending plans for 2030-31, according to the Institute for Fiscal Studies. That is before taking into account an additional £11bn needed to fund a commitment to increase defence spending to 3% of GDP.

Official figures on Wednesday showed inflation in the UK rose in October to 3.6% amid the global surge in energy prices triggered by the Iran war. Economic forecasters predict a further rise in inflation, with the Bank of England anticipating a peak of close to 5% next year.

Threadneedle Street raised interest rates from 3.75% to 4% earlier this month and warned further increases might be required to combat inflationary pressures unleashed by the Iran war. Financial markets predict three quarter-point rate increases before the end of next year.

Rob Wood, the chief UK economist at the consultancy Pantheon Macroeconomics, said: “The October budget did little to address the more serious challenges facing the public finances, so we continue to have doubts about the government’s ability to follow through on its fiscal plans, suggesting upside risks to borrowing in the coming years.”

stories.body:
State attorney says scandal ‘raises bright red flags’ and aims to find out if company misled investors

California has served an investigative subpoena on Nvidia after a scandal that prompted the departure of co-founder and longtime chief executive Jensen Huang.

Rob Bonta, the US state’s attorney general, issued the subpoena as part of an investigation into whether exports of the California-based company’s advanced semiconductor chips ended up in China, contravening US restrictions.

“The conduct of Nvidia and its former chief executive raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors,” said Bonta.

“Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: companies cannot mislead their investors.”

The subpoena, issued on Thursday, followed Huang’s resignation a week ago after it emerged he had multiple affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy.

Alice Huang, who is not related, is associated with Singapore-based Megaspeed, which has bought nearly $5bn (£3.8bn) of Nvidia chips and hardware in recent years, and is being investigated for possibly diverting advanced restricted chips to China .

Megaspeed has said it is a “legitimate and lawful” business, and that Huang left the company late last year.

Bonta said the investigation would also look at whether the former Nvidia chief’s actions resulted in confidential information being passed to China.

“My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang’s actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information,” he said. “And if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law.”

Nvidia’s shares are down by a fifth since Huang admitted the extramarital affair, hitting a one-year low at the close of trading on Thursday, and wiping almost $1tn off its market value.

Earlier this week, Harvey Jones, Nvidia’s chair, said the company had no intention of reinstating Huang after the former CEO said he would be “honoured” to return. Elon Musk and a host of tech bosses had campaigned for Nvidia to bring him back .

Huang is due to testify before several congressional committees over the potential breach of national security on 1 December.

after newsletter promotion

Shares in rival chipmaker AMD closed down almost 8% on Thursday after the publication of reports connected to short seller Hunterbrook warning about its links to China and the “circular financing” of customers.

The company, which has been targeted amid the Nvidia scandal, is looking at a further fall of more than 5% in pre-market trading.

Hunterbrook Media published allegations on the use of AMD’s software by a Chinese server maker blacklisted by the US. Sister publication, The Bear Cave newsletter, alleged that AMD’s use of datacentre lease guarantees and backstops for unsold cloud computing capacity could leave it exposed to a pullback in AI spending.

AMD said the reports’ claims “misrepresent AMD’s business practices and relationships”.

“AMD complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations,” the company said. “We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity.”

AMD’s share price has more than doubled so far this year, giving the company a market capitalisation of more than $800m.
